stories.body:
The latest UN climate summit, Cop31, will get underway in Antalya, Turkey, on November 9. One of its key objectives is to boost electrification across the global economy – replacing petrol and diesel vehicles, gas boilers and some industrial processes that burn fossil fuels with electric alternatives.

The summit’s host, Turkey, has set a target of 35% of energy demand being met by electricity by 2035, up from around 20% today. Announcing the “35-by-35” pledge, Cop31 president Murat Kurum described it as “one of the defining features” of Turkey’s presidency, highlighting the risks of continued dependence on imported fossil fuels .

Without doubt, electrification is essential to curtailing greenhouse gas emissions, and is already gathering pace. The International Energy Agency (IEA) has declared we are living in the “age of electricity” , and if stated policy pledges hold, global electrification rates will hit 31% by 2050. The Cop31’s focus on electrification hopes to build upon and accelerate this existing trend.

But electrification alone won’t deliver a clean energy transition. Two major challenges remain: the continued expansion of fossil fuel production, and growing geopolitical competition over clean technologies where the latter is increasingly shaping governments’ climate and energy policies, as they struggle to compete with dominant “electrostates” such as China.

Silence on supply

The Australian climate minister and Cop31’s president of negotiations has described electrification and fossil fuel reduction as “different sides of the same coin” . But they are not interchangeable. Electrification can reduce some demand for fossil fuels, but it won’t stop governments approving new projects and expanding supply.

By 2030, governments are planning to produce more than double the amount of fossil fuels than would be consistent with limiting warning to 1.5°C. More concerning is that this assessment was made before the conflict and disruption in the Middle East, which has caused the US, Brazil, Guyana, Argentina, Canada and other fossil fuel producers to increase output in the name of energy security. The UK, meanwhile, has approved the Jackdaw gasfield in a purported bid to protect jobs and keep homes warm.

The 35-by-35 target is also silent on where that additional electricity will come from. After all, a country could in theory increase its rate of electrification by burning more fossil fuels (imagine a country where every car was electric, but all that electricity came from coal).

A genuine energy transition

What’s needed is the two-pronged approach of electrifying economies while simultaneously phasing out fossil fuels and reducing their supply. This will ensure capital is reallocated to renewable energy for electrification. Governments can do this nationally or through international initiatives such as the Beyond Oil and Gas Alliance , the Clean Energy Transition Partnership and the Cop-adjacent conference on Transitioning Away from Fossil Fuels .

Skirting the fossil fuel issue is nothing new at these summits. It took 26 years for a formal resolution or agreement to explicitly name fossil fuels, in Glasgow in 2021 . And even then it only passed with calls to “phasedown” unabated coal power and phase-out “inefficient” fossil fuel subsidies.

At Cop31, fossil fuels are entirely absent from the formal agenda . Brazil has published an extensive voluntary “roadmap” to guide governments’ phase-out efforts, but this sits outside the formal negotiations and lacks timelines .

This begs the question: is a focus on electrification a way to avoid the perennially thorny issue of fossil fuels?

Just electrify everything

Even growing demand for electricity does not guarantee a clean energy transition. The data centre boom in the US and beyond, for instance, is driving the use of gas and coal to generate electricity. The International Gas Union, a lobby group for natural gas producers, is explicitly positioning gas as a way to meet growing demand from data centres and AI.

Increasing electrification looks relatively straightforward: just encourage more renewable energy production and electric vehicles . Yet, for most of the world, this would mean overcoming security and trade tensions with China, whose dominance in clean technologies, manufacturing and rare earth processing makes it a lynchpin electrostate in a world hoping to electrify everything.

China’s dominance is near total. For the component materials of solar panels, in 2024 China controlled 93% of global polysilicon processing, 97% of wafer manufacturing – making the thin slices of silicon that form the basis of solar panels – 92% of solar cell manufacturing and 86% of solar module production. It also produced more than 80% of electric vehicle batteries in 2025. According to the IEA, China is dominant across 19 of 20 energy-related strategic minerals, averaging over 70% of processing control. Achieving global electrification targets will therefore require continued access to Chinese technologies, products and raw materials.

This runs counter to almost two decades of western policy aimed at protecting domestic industries from Chinese competition and restricting China’s technological development, most notably with semi-conductors . While these efforts have largely failed to contain Chinese innovation, an overreliance on Chinese clean technologies is increasingly seen as a “serious risk” to Europe’s economic and national security. European governments have responded with tariffs and restrictions on Chinese imports and investments, while seeking to build up their own manufacturing capacity.

Governments face a difficult dilemma. Opening their economies further to Chinese technologies could mean unpicking trade protections developed over years and create new dependencies, while refusing to cooperate with China risks slowing electrification and may even drive some governments to abandon climate and energy policies altogether because they cannot compete.

While the drive towards electrification at Cop31 is to be welcomed, it cannot be a substitute for the harder political task of securing binding commitments to phase out fossil fuels, fast and fairly.

stories.body:
Democrats won back the Texas House for the first time in 24 years. Gov. Greg Abbott’s bullishness on vouchers turned off some Republican voters in rural communities that have historically been strongholds for his party, politicians said.

Co-published with The Texas Tribune

Texas Gov. Greg Abbott’s vision for education was finally coming together.

This year, the state launched a voucher program that allowed roughly 110,000 of Texas’ more than 5 million schoolchildren to get a private education using taxpayer dollars. Abbott’s loyal appointee at the Texas Education Agency, Commissioner Mike Morath, was leading the state’s largest takeover of public schools in recent history . And the Texas State Board of Education, with Abbott’s support , helped pass a controversial new social studies curriculum that required teaching Bible stories and shifted away from world history to focus on Texas and the United States.

On Tuesday night, as Democrats clinched nearly every office in the state, it all began to unravel.

In a speech after denying Abbott a fourth term, Texas Gov.-elect Gina Hinojosa called for a reversal of his education agenda. She pledged to fire Morath and to end the public school takeovers.

Perhaps most significantly, she doubled down on a campaign promise to erase one of Abbott’s biggest accomplishments: school vouchers.

“We will work tirelessly to repair the damage of the Texas voucher scam,” said Hinojosa, who did not respond to requests for an interview.

It is not clear how Hinojosa will deliver on that promise. While Democrats have the ability to restrict parts of the program, eliminating it would require legislative action.

But Hinojosa will have help.

Democrat Sarah Eckhardt, a former state senator who voted against vouchers and will now lead the state office charged with running the program, has said she will push changes to increase accountability and transparency.

Eckhardt, however, acknowledged the limitations of her office, saying that any big overhaul must come from lawmakers.

Democrats won back the Texas House for the first time in 24 years, but Republicans retained a majority in the Senate.

Rep. Diego Bernal, the Democratic vice chair of the House education committee, seemed confident that there is a path toward killing the program, at least as it now exists.

Bernal, whose district is in San Antonio, said some Republican colleagues previously told him privately that they had reservations about the voucher program, but were limited in what they could do because of pressure from leaders who have now been ousted.

“I guarantee that program is not going to be untouched, and it will be probably unrecognizable, if not extinct, by the time we’re done with it,” he said.

Rural Texas Pushes Back

Abbott spent years trying to pass a statewide voucher program. By 2024, he’d grown angry at rural Republicans who repeatedly blocked such legislation because, they argued, public schools were a vital part of their communities. So Abbott shelled out millions of dollars to oust them from office and elect pro-voucher Republicans instead.

He succeeded. And the following year, those Republicans helped pass the $1 billion state voucher program. This week, at least 13 Republicans who Abbott had previously endorsed or helped fund as part of his voucher push lost to Democrats or were trailing in close races.

Abbott’s office declined an interview request, referring ProPublica and The Texas Tribune to his campaign office, which did not respond.

His bullishness on vouchers turned off some Republican voters in rural communities that have historically been strongholds for his party, education experts and politicians said.

A Texas Tribune analysis found Democrats made striking gains in rural and semirural parts of the state , where concern over vouchers, along with issues like data centers, ran high. In rural counties, Abbott’s margin over Hinojosa fell 16 percentage points from his 2022 margin over former U.S. Rep. Beto O’Rourke, and it fell 20 percentage points in exurban counties.

Former state Rep. Dewayne Burns, an anti-voucher Republican from a mostly rural district south of Fort Worth who was defeated by an Abbott-backed primary challenger in 2024, said many of his constituents felt betrayed by the governor’s push for vouchers. “That’s the first time that I think rural Texans really kind of stepped back and said, ‘Are you guys really supporting us?’” he said. “I think they overestimated the loyalty that Texans, especially rural Texans, had to the governor.”

Former state Rep. Steve Allison, who represented a suburban San Antonio district before he was unseated in the 2024 primary, said he remains convinced his constituents never wanted the voucher system. Pro-voucher groups targeted him in a series of ads that attacked him for issues like border security and property taxes but said little about school choice. Polls at the time showed Texans held complicated views on school choice, with one University of Houston poll showing that while two-thirds of Texans supported voucher legislation, an equal number believed that vouchers would funnel money away from already struggling public schools.

“I know what I saw when my staff took very careful notice of what phone calls were coming in and what emails and texts and visits were coming in,” he said in an interview. “It was clear that the overall district was opposed to vouchers.”

Concerns about vouchers became key in several rural and suburban Texas districts this year where Abbott’s selected candidates had won two years ago. One of those races was for Allison’s old seat, which pro-voucher candidate Marc LaHood won in 2024 after Abbott spent at least $700,000 supporting him.

Another was in Bell County in Central Texas. There, the Abbott-backed incumbent, Rep. Hillary Hickland, conceded a close race Wednesday morning. She did not respond to a request for an interview. Her Democratic opponent, Amelia Rabroker, a former teacher, said the Republicans’ heavy-handed push for vouchers spurred her to challenge Hickland.

“A lot of money was pushed into her campaign to make that happen, and she delivered on those vouchers, and it was very upsetting to the people of Central Texas,” Rabroker said. “I think it was a huge concern. The biggest.”

Similarly, LaHood, who did not respond to requests for comment, faced a flurry of questions over his support of vouchers at a candidate forum for the District 121 race in October. His opponent, Democrat Zack Dunn, said vouchers and public education were second only to affordability in the minds of voters he met. On Tuesday night, Dunn defeated LaHood with 54% of vote.

“Across the board, overwhelmingly the sentiment was, ‘We need to fully fund our public schools,’” Dunn said in an interview. “The voucher scam, the voucher scheme, the voucher vote that was taken is hurting us. It’s hurting us definitely across the state, but it’s hurting us in 121. Yes, we heard that over and over and over again.”

What’s Next?

Dunn said he would support measures that ensure more transparency in how taxpayer dollars are used for private schools.

Ultimately, though, he wants to see the program repealed.

Some changes can come through administrative actions by Eckhardt, the new state comptroller. In a news conference the day after her election, Eckhardt said she planned to rigorously audit how taxpayer money is spent and to release more information about the program to the public.

Under her Republican predecessors, the comptroller’s office shielded information that included data detailing how much state funding certain private schools received and how many students most public schools lost to the program. The office argued that it was protecting student privacy.

“As the comptroller, my job is to vigorously follow the money and report back to the Legislature if their investment is not panning out,” Eckhardt said. She added, “That is part of the vigorous audit and performance evaluation of this program that any comptroller should be doing, and I certainly will be doing.”

One key supporter of vouchers in the Senate, the last Republican bulwark in the state, is taking a more measured approach on the program’s future.

Houston Republican Sen. Paul Bettencourt, who led the effort to approve vouchers that had failed in prior years, said the Legislature will need to review the outcomes from the 2026-27 school year and assess the benefits and families’ concerns. He pointed to the fact that vouchers were returned by some parents whose children required special education services.

“I think that it has helped students in many other states,” Bettencourt said. “We need to look at what’s happened here with this first cohort, and we need to make sure that we’re debating not the emotionality prior to passage of a bill, but the facts of what happened after the passage of a bill.”

Scott Schneider, an attorney who represents private schools participating in the voucher program, said the midterm results shocked private school leaders. Some were counting on the state funding to support their business. He said private school leaders could start a lobbying effort to grandfather in the families already benefiting from the program, but schools are also planning for what they will do if the state funding goes away altogether.

“It’s going to be a hot mess,” Schneider said.

stories.body:
A Closer Look

From rallies in Ohio to a Pennsylvania voting site on Election Day, the tone had noticeably changed among voters in some of the regions that were crucial to electing Donald Trump.

Jacob Hawk leaned over the plastic fencing to get Vivek Ramaswamy’s attention as the Republican candidate for Ohio governor moved down the line shaking hands at the Ohio University branch campus in Chillicothe, six days before the midterm elections. Hawk held onto Ramaswamy’s hand and started trying to tell him everything he was dealing with, everything he wanted the Republican candidates gathered there to help him with.

Hawk, 39, told him that he was a self-employed landscaper who was having a hard time with the high cost of fuel. He told him that he was raising three young kids from two different moms, mostly on his own. He told him of his worries for his 9-year-old son, who was autistic and underweight and suffered from a two-year delay in brain development.

Ramaswamy, a biotech billionaire, nodded and offered some token reassurance and moved down the line, toward the arena where he would soon be appearing with President Donald Trump and Sen. Jon Husted and the rest of the Republican slate in a state that Trump had won by 11 percentage points two years ago, and which the party had dominated during the era of Trump. I had been at many Republican events in the state over that time, including a rally in an airplane hangar outside Dayton in March 2016, where a giant crowd had roared as Trump’s jet had rolled into view and where he had declared that he had come to save Ohio. “Our jobs are being sucked away,” he said then. “It’s unbelievable what’s happening.”

This event was different. Ten years had passed, and gone was the fierce bravado of Trump the conquering hero, bristling with retribution and promises. This rally was populated largely by the same sort of voters who had been particularly drawn to Trump all along , working-class Midwesterners who had not been engaged in politics before he came on the scene. But there were fewer of them — the campaign had chosen an arena that held only 2,000 — and their devotion had been subsumed by uncertainty. They were still with Trump, but they weren’t sure how to reconcile their own difficulties with the fact that he was the president during this trying time.

Take gas prices, which “are beating the hell out of me,” Hawk told me. He was trying his best not to hold them against Trump and his decision to go to war against Iran, instead faulting Congress for limiting domestic oil drilling. “The president has to go find oil in another country because Congress won’t let him find it in our country,” he said, overlooking the fact that Trump’s party has controlled both houses of Congress during his second term.

Nearby, Debbie Shock, a 57-year-old mail carrier, blamed the high fuel costs on “the stock exchange, the markets — they’re the ones that control it.” “We have oil right here in the U.S.,” she said. “Why are we buying it from other countries to begin with?”

Shock fit a profile I had gotten to know well in 2016: an Obama-Trump voter. She was loyal to Trump — “I like the man. Nobody’s perfect, you know what I mean?” — and told me she would never go back to Democrats now. Why not? I asked. “They’re covering up the child molestation,” she said. What did she mean by that? “I’ve heard stories about the sex trafficking. The Clintons are involved in it, Disney World, you know, all that.”

It would be easy to ridicule such murky talk, yet it was not much less coherent than what soon emerged on the arena stage, which was streamed on a large screen for the few hundred of us who were out on the lawn outside the arena. Trump has never been known for structured oratory, but it is hard to overstate the extent to which his digressive style has advanced since 2016, and to convey how surreal it is to experience firsthand, as the reality of what presidential communication has come to in 2026.

The rally opened with the customary introductory video of late-era Trump, an explicitly messianic framing: “God said, ‘I need someone who will be strong and courageous,’” the voice-over intones. “So God made Trump.”

Thus introduced, Trump opened his remarks with a lengthy disquisition on Husted’s body, which had newly become part of his routine. “I looked at Jon and studied his physique,” he cooed, after referring to his recent comments on Husted’s “ass.” “I studied the feet, the legs, the shoulders. I tapped him on the shoulder, and it was like hitting a piece of steel.”

When a protester inside the arena started shouting something — those of us outside couldn’t hear what — and was removed, Trump bid him good riddance: “Now he goes home and his boyfriend gets upset with him.”

There were protesters outside, too, and things were starting to heat up between them and the supporters. “What are you talking about, ‘boyfriend?’” shouted one protester, a young man. “He was just talking about Jon Husted’s ass! That’s not gay??”

A supporter in front of me, a bearded man in his 50s, stewed as he watched the protesters. “You’re going to see someone dropping like a bad habit,” he growled, as he started to move toward them, before being held back by the woman who was with him.

A moment later, Trump had moved on to Jeffrey Epstein, saying that the Democrats had protected him for years. “I threw Jeffrey Epstein the hell out of Mar-a-Lago,” he declared. “I was the one who was totally exonerated from him. But they use it, because that’s what they do. They’re sick, weak people.”

This set off a new round of shouting outside, as cries of “pedophiles!” flew back and forth.

Suddenly, one Trump supporter near me rushed hard at a protester and knocked him to the ground, his head landing with such a thud on the blacktop that I initially thought it might be a suppressed gunshot. Dozens of officers swarmed to the spot. Cameras flashed.

A few moments later, a couple other protesters, also young men, began railing against the war against Iran. “We’re going to be the ones sent off to die for Israel,” one shouted. “‘America First,’ and you want me to die in the Middle East?”

Trump touched on the war — “they’re getting beaten very badly” — but spent far more time on his home renovations. “The White House has to be beautiful outside, it needs that exterior plaster. The bricks were falling, the stone was broken, the monuments were coming off, the beautiful windows were cracked, it looked terrible, and I fixed it very inexpensively, and now it’s more beautiful than ever,” he said. “And President Obama, who doesn’t understand cleanliness, who doesn’t understand broken cracked stone and sidewalks, who doesn’t understand that having asphalt going to your main entrance is not the right thing, we’d like to have granite and marble we’d like to have it look nice, you don’t use asphalt, you use asphalt for your streets. …”

On the ramble went. To the Haitians in nearby Springfield: “The town went from no crime to high crime,” but “they’re being moved out.” To a riff on Ramaswamy’s ad featuring his opponent Amy Acton’s mother calling her a liar, in apparent reference to Acton’s having accused her stepfather of raping her when she was 12, as he was subsequently charged with doing. The ad had met with widespread opprobrium, but Trump defended Ramaswamy. “The mother said that Amy Acton, the daughter, is a liar, that she is no good. … How the hell is that his problem?” To “O Canada, which has been ripping us off for years,” and Somalia, “which isn’t even a country,” and “transgender mutilization,” and his plan to rename the Strait of Hormuz for himself.

Finally, Trump ceded the stage to Husted and Ramaswamy. But by then, the lawn had emptied out as people drifted home, Jacob Hawk among them. A vendor was shouting out discount prices on his MAGA merchandise. “$10 special on hats! All the hats are $10! These are normally $25 hats. That’s a good hat for $10.”

The next day, the full Republican slate of statewide candidates appeared, sans Trump, at a small pep rally inside a former Delphi auto-parts factory in Vandalia, outside Dayton. It is an enormous building that employed more than 100 prior to its closing in 2009 and is now being used as a warehouse by a company that sells air conditioners, employing only 10 or so; Delphi announcements still remained on the bulletin boards, adding a ghostly feel.

The setting was an unintentional reminder of what Ohio has been through. Between 2000 and 2025, the state lost 300,000 manufacturing jobs, a devastation that had made it highly susceptible to Trump’s message in 2016. But Republicans have been in charge of the state since 2010, and so it was the task of the candidates gathered there, with an audience of just a few dozen, to cast the state as being on an upswing. Complicating this challenge is the fact that so much of the state’s recent growth has been concentrated in the Columbus area: countless data centers, defense contractor Anduril, a massive Intel plant under construction.

The bigger challenge, though, was the nationwide pall that hung over the event: the reality of stubbornly high inflation and high gas prices, the latter a direct consequence of Trump’s decision to go to war with Iran. He had stood against costly foreign entanglements when he ran in 2016, in opposition to his party’s recent record, and carried that same banner again in 2024. But another aspect of his political persona had prevailed: a heedless swagger that, in this case, had been fanned by Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth. It had led him into this drawn-out conflict that has already cost U.S. taxpayers more than $47 billion.

And it had left a long row of Republican candidates standing in this giant building stacked high with made-in-China air conditioners all but pleading the small assemblage to save them from the political climate. “You can’t give up,” Husted said. “This is a Republican state, and the only way Democrats can win is if Republicans don’t vote.”

Five days later, I was in York County, Pennsylvania, which Trump had won by 25 points in 2024, and which was home to one of four Republican-held House districts targeted by Democrats. I chose to go to a precinct on the outskirts of York, thinking it would offer a diverse cross-section, in between more Democratic York proper and more Republican rural areas. But over 90 minutes of conversations, I didn’t encounter a Republican voter until I was about to call it a day.

The first person I spoke with, Bill, a 52-year-old state government employee who asked that I not use his last name for fear of losing his job, had voted for Trump three times. He hardly considered himself MAGA but was drawn in 2016 to Trump’s “drain the swamp” rhetoric and his disavowal of the war in Iraq. He voted for him again in 2020 and 2024 because he didn’t think much of Joe Biden and Kamala Harris.

But on this day, Bill was coming to vote against his Republican representative, Scott Perry, because he was too “Trump adjacent.” Bill had finally had enough of Trump, especially when it came to all the revelations of self-dealing involving his family and cronies. “I will not be falling for him again,” he told me. “Drain the swamp, no wars. … It was all a lie.”

He said he couldn’t understand how Trump had gone from America First to seemingly letting the country’s foreign policy be dictated by Israel. He said that he was voting for the Democrats mainly just for the sake of “gridlock,” as deliberate blockage. “Someone’s got to stop this,” he said. “It’s getting out of control.”

Each Democratic voter I spoke with after that was coming with their own motivation for voting against the Republican slate, like the cast of “Murder on the Orient Express.”

For Annie (who also asked that I not use her last name), it was for Trump’s social-welfare cuts, which had cost her and her disabled husband $300 per month in SNAP benefits and nearly cost them their Medicaid coverage.

For Desiree Edmonds, an elementary school teacher, it was high inflation, which was translating into anxiety among the working-class children in her classroom.

For Mark Castillo, a 19-year-old ironworker, it was for the sky-high cost of diesel.

For Jacqueline Jimenez, a native Puerto Rican who worked as a home-health aide, it was for the excessive harshness of ICE arrests.

For Shiri Kramer, a warehouse worker, it was for the general meanness emanating from the administration, which made her think of her grandfather, a Jewish American who had extended mercy to German POWs during World War II. “My grandfather would be writhing right now,” she said. “Nothing happening in our country is OK.”

By night’s end, Republicans had lost this Pennsylvania district by 10 points, as well as the other three in the state and more than 40 nationwide. They had lost at least seven Senate seats, even in states where Democrats hadn’t prevailed in decades — Kansas, Texas, South Carolina. Incredibly, even Mississippi was on the verge. In Ohio, Republicans lost the race for Senate and governor — only one of the seven statewide candidates on stage at the warehouse emerged a victor — as well as two Republican-held House seats, a stark reversal in a state that had seemed to be trending away from Democrats for good. In all, Democrats flipped five governorships and up to 12 state legislative chambers. The Democratic popular-vote margin in congressional races nationwide was 13 percentage points — nearly double the Republican margin in their own wave years of 2010 and 1994, and approaching the scale of the historic Democratic rout in the post-Watergate election of 1974.

The particularly stunning loss of the South Carolina seat brought to mind a warning issued in May 2016 by Lindsey Graham, whose death this July left the seat vacant. “If we nominate Trump, we will get destroyed…….and we will deserve it,” Graham tweeted in 2016. For years, the Republican Party had avoided the catastrophic reckoning he warned of — through Trump’s narrow win in 2016, through the Jan. 6, 2021, assault on the Capitol , through Biden’s fateful insistence on running for reelection at age 81 in 2024. Along the way, much of the party, including Graham himself, had accommodated itself to Trump. One way of looking at the 2026 results was that the warning had finally come true. The reckoning had been delayed by a decade, but it had gathered more force over time, like a boulder rolling downhill.

There was a hint of such a reckoning in the words that Bill, the three-time Trump voter, left me with in York. After he returned from voting, he bade me farewell with a parting regret.

“You see what’s going on,” he said, “and you’re like, ‘What the hell did I do?’”

stories.title: How Moscow Is Reacting to the U.S. Midterms
stories.summary: Russian media coverage of the Democratic midterm victory reveals Moscow’s concerns about renewed support for Ukraine amid hopes for political gridlock in Washington. The post How Moscow Is Reacting to the U.S. Midterms appeared first on Foreign Policy In Focus .
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
U.S. President Donald Trump (R) walks with Russian President Vladimir Putin as they arrives at Joint Base Elmendorf-Richardson on August 15, 2025 in Anchorage, Alaska. (Andrew Harnik/Getty Images)

Governments across the globe have expressed varied responses to the GOP’s stunning midterm defeat as Democrats are poised to take control of the House and Senate in just a couple of months. Russia’s media outlets have been reporting on the results with a focus on how the altered congressional landscape might impact U.S.-Russia relations, particularly regarding the war in Ukraine. Since Moscow often deploys media statements as trial balloons to gauge which narratives resonate with the public, Russia watchers should take heed of the midterm explanations that are making the rounds of Russian state-owned and pro-Kremlin news services, and what purpose these narratives might serve.

The government-owned news organization RIA Novosti observed that the blue wave heralded the end of Trumpism, concluding, “None of this bodes well for Russia. Full control of Congress will allow the Democrats to push pro-Ukrainian and anti-Russian legislation and to secure funding for Kyiv in the budget. Under Trump, the United States ruled out directly supplying weapons to the Ukrainian Armed Forces. Now, [weapons supplies] will most likely be renewed, and all the president’s initiatives are doomed to fail.”

The pro-Kremlin newspaper Vedomosti tapped political analyst Dmitrii Novikov for his take on the elections, who similarly prognosticated that Democrats will aim to pass legislation committing the United States to providing security guarantees to Ukraine. “If the Trump administration doesn’t avoid this effort,” Novikov warned, “the Democrats in Congress may well try to insert additional obligations regarding Kyiv to the [potential legislation], both in terms of language and additional military and economic aid.”

These observations are not far off from Democrats’ stated intentions. For example, newly elected Democratic senators James Talarico and Abdul El-Sayed, who won Senate races in Texas and Michigan respectively, have both expressed strong support for economic and military assistance to Ukraine, with Talarico arguing that continued aid is a “ cost-saving measure ” and El-Sayed casting the conflict as “ a war between democracy and autocracy ” in a 2022 op-ed. Their position is consistent with Democratic and bipartisan efforts during Trump’s second term to expand Ukraine aid and strengthen sanctions against Russia, many of which met have with GOP opposition. Bills like Rep. Gregory Meeks’s Prohibit Corrupt Russia Oil Deals Act, which seeks to reverse the Trump-brokered diesel agreement with Russia and has already received bipartisan support, are likely to gain momentum in both chambers come January.

However, if a Democrat-controlled Congress succeeds in constraining the president’s policy objectives on Ukraine, Trump may behave more chaotically on the world stage, not least because dealing with opposition is not his forte. Prevented from carrying out his domestic agenda, Trump may well seek to achieve his goals in the foreign policy sphere, where since 9/11 the executive has accumulated more power to pursue its aims, such as heading diplomacy efforts and military operations, with limited congressional involvement. Post-election, Trump has reminded voters of his veto authority, which Congress can only override with two-thirds majorities in both chambers, and which the Democrats do not have.

In its analysis of the U.S. midterms, the Kremlin-aligned Lenta.ru news site made a similar observation , with political analyst Georgii Asatrian predicting that a frustrated American president is more likely to focus on the international arena: “A paradox is possible: the president will try to compensate for his limitations within the country by increased foreign policy activity.’” Political scientist Anastasia Gafarova told Kremlin-aligned Gazeta.ru the same thing : “Given his severely weakened domestic political powers, it seems Trump will try to achieve historic successes precisely in that dimension which is institutionally more vested in the executive branch, namely, foreign policy.”

A far more defiant note was struck by the state-controlled media organization RT, which insisted that U.S. policy toward Ukraine and Russia is unlikely to change. Associate Professor at RUDN University Nikolai Parkhit’ko told RT : “It’s too early to talk about a landslide Democratic victory. […] The Democratic Party has sensible politicians who are discussing reducing aid [to Ukraine] which comes primarily from the pockets of American taxpayers. Kyiv is celebrating right now, as though Ukraine has flown to Venus and the rest of us are all left here to die. But it’s utterly immature and ill-conceived to think that tomorrow Zelensky will be given a trillion dollars, it’s shortsighted.” Although there are no Democrats who publicly discuss reducing Ukraine aid, this sally aligns with similar RT efforts that target U.S. voters as part of wider influence operations that weave populist grievances into pro-Russian narratives, in this case lamenting the loss of hard-earned American tax dollars in order to undermine public support for Ukraine.

The media assessments vary because they serve different purposes. If Russia is unable to achieve its objectives in Ukraine or make dialogue breakthroughs with Washington, it will be convenient to blame Democratic interference and military support for Kyiv. At the same time, the coverage reassures Russian readers that Trump ultimately has final say over U.S.-Russia relations, and even if he didn’t, Moscow’s decision-making does not rely on political shifts in Washington. After all, although Russia has often regarded Trump as useful, its most recent foreign policy concept has assessed that the United States seeks to weaken Russia and undermine its economic and technological capabilities while threatening its sovereignty and territorial integrity.

Finally, the repeated prophecy in pro-Russian news outlets of escalating tensions between the U.S. Congress and a president who, they insist, will be aggressively focused on making unilateral foreign policy decisions that undermine the Democratic agenda, is consistent with the Kremlin’s own preference for American disruption, distraction, and gridlock. The more disunited and dysfunctional the American government is, the less effective it will be in challenging Russian ambitions.

stories.title: Democrats Should Not Revert To The Status Quo Ante
stories.summary: The post Democrats Should Not Revert To The Status Quo Ante appeared first on NOEMA .

stories.body:
It’s time for a new governing vision.

Nathan Gardels is the editor-in-chief of Noema Magazine. He is also the co-founder of and a senior adviser to the Berggruen Institute.

The great blue wave that washed over America in the election should not lure Democrats into the delusion that they are once again lovingly embraced by the body politic.

Rather, it should be seen for what it is: a widespread counter-revolt at the ballot box against all that Trumpism has wrought — a heightened crisis of affordability exacerbated by trade wars and a war of choice with Iran, self-dealing corruption, politicization of the rule of law and an unbounded, mean-spirited mega-megalomania rarely seen in mature democracies.

The worst mistake Democrats can make is to misread their mandate. That mandate is to narrow the margin of maneuver of a wounded lame-duck presidency, derail the trajectory toward autocracy and clean up the mess. It is not to return to the status quo ante of cultural elitism, censorious identity politics, lax borders and hyper-globalization that opened the path to Trumpism in the first place.

Above all, what Americans are looking for is not so different than what the Gen Z uprisings erupting across Europe and South Asia these days are seeking: to restore trust in the fairness of governing institutions and unclog the routes of opportunity and upward mobility by tackling inequality at the root of the affordability crisis.

With the double failure of the old Democratic agenda and now the Trumpist alternative, the 2028 presidential contest will be the next chance for a new governing vision to emerge in the United States.

Whatever else such a vision may encompass, there are two structural changes that are imperative to ensuring that an anxious and alienated public will have a real say and a clear stake in their future.

First, the only way out of social polarization and the appeal of autocracy is a deeper institutional culture of engagement in which citizens themselves are involved — outside the divisive passions of the partisan electoral arena — in setting the rules that govern their lives. In other words, participation without populism.

Second, mending the fissures of democracy will only be possible if the growing concentration of wealth at the top generated by the arriving AI economy is more widely shared.

We have written about this often in Noema, but I will restate the case in the new context of the latest turn in American politics.

Sharing The AI Wealth

Much of the driving force of politics to come is a pervasive sense of gross inequality, that chances are no longer fair and those with connections and assets are accelerating away from the average family, which is only falling behind with no hope of catching up. Upward mobility has become a mirage. For too many, the good life is receding beyond reach.

Those who revolted against a cultural elite they viewed as looking down on them found themselves faced instead with a politically connected economic elite more entrenched and consolidated than ever before in post-World War II America.

As a result, there is an upswelling reaction from below. Those across America’s various electoral contests voting for “democratic socialists” are not hardened partisans of an old ideology. They are only a broad constituency realizing that capitalism is not working for them; that the benefits of how our system works, supercharged by digital technology, go to those who are already rich and getting richer because they own the assets that are growing in value.

If the pervasive sense of gross inequality is a key driver of social and political division, then the answer is broader wealth sharing so all Americans are pulling in the same direction.

This is where the idea of “universal basic capital” comes in.

AI innovations are increasingly decoupling productivity growth and wealth creation from employment and income, widening the inequality gap between those who “own the robots” and those who labor for their livelihood. Read Noema in print.

The value of productivity growth associated with AI is accruing to those with financial assets that are ballooning on the tail of Big Tech, concentrating wealth at the pinnacle. The top 10% own 93% of all equities.

Despite the immediate post-election market turmoil, regulation on safety and data center-related energy concerns expected from the new Congress will, in the end, temper the justified worries of the public about AI. While slowing down the pace of the race to the frontier of superintelligence, it will incentivize the kind of practical applications we’ve seen in China that will boost productivity across the economy.

A new social contract that responds to this dynamic would foster an ownership share for all in the wealth generated by intelligent machines that portend the displacement of gainful employment and wage depression as AI penetrates the entire economy. After all, it is the general intellect — the public’s personal data — that is the raw material transmuted by algorithms into a productive asset. If wealth is produced by all, all should share in its value.

“The worst mistake Democrats can make is to misread their mandate.”

This can be done mostly through universal savings/investment accounts for families and individuals seeded by an innovation levy on companies across the AI economy. The idea is not only to break up concentration of wealth at the top but to also build it from below. The best way to fight inequality in the digital age is to spread the equity around.

Thinking Outside The Ballot Box

The connective tissue of democracy has seriously decayed in recent years as trust in impartial institutions has hit rock bottom and the public square splinters into social media silos.

The triumph of Trumpism was not the cause of this crisis of governance. It was a symptom of the decay of democratic institutions that, captured by the organized special interests of an insider establishment, failed to address the dislocations of globalization and the disruptions of rapid technological change. To add danger to decay, the fevered partisans of populism all too readily threw out the baby with the bathwater, assaulting the very integrity of institutional checks and balances that guarantee the enduring survival of republics. The revolt against a moribund political class transmuted into a revolt against governance itself.

Since neither the stakeholders of the old status quo nor the upstarts of populism have offered any effective, systemic solutions to what ails the nation, protracted polarization and paralysis set in.

In the end, there are only two solutions to this predicament — the move Trump has made toward strongman autocracy, or thinking outside the ballot box by inviting the broader civil society into governance through new mediating institutions of citizen engagement that complement representative government.

One reparative response, embryonic but indicative of the larger possibility, has been introduced in California: a first-in-the-nation online public platform to help bridge silos and mend the breach of distrust between the public and the institutions of self-government. The platform, called Engaged California (EC), encourages and facilitates the direct engagement of citizens with government and with each other.

Engaged California is not glorified polling and is more than a town hall gathering. It is a three-way tool that enables policymakers and administrators to listen at scale to average citizens outside of election cycles and be responsive; it invites citizens to directly voice their concerns and proposals on an ongoing basis; and it is a platform for Californians from all walks of life to interact with each other to find common ground.

AI serves as a sorting tool to register consensus among thousands of participants on priorities for government action and to collate fresh ideas that emerge from this practice of collective intelligence.

In short, it is exactly this kind of innovative institutional platform for “governing with the people” that can restore trust because the public itself is proactively engaged.

Beyond Tinkering

Since the great transformations underway in America today are systemic in nature, so too must new ways and means of governance go beyond tinkering around the edges of waning ways that no longer fit the times.

Governance is how communities invent and shape their destiny. It determines whether a society goes forward or backward. Like the homeostasis of all organisms, governance is the regulator, arbiter and navigator of human affairs. It processes emotions through reason, as the means by which societies not only survive but thrive by adapting to change.

Going forward in this light, democratic practices and institutions must adapt to the unprecedented scale of connectivity in a way that fosters a governing consensus instead of dividing the body politic against itself. In an AI economy, where massive new wealth is being generated by mining the general intellect of public data and transforming it into a productive asset, the old industrial division between labor and capital diminishes and everyone must become an owner sharing fairly in that wealth.

With the old slate now wiped clean by failed alternatives, the space is opening once again for the political imagination to think anew with a systemic response to the challenges at hand. The blue wave rebuke of Trumpism puts the onus on Democrats.

stories.title: How This Year's Super El Niño Will Worsen Global Hunger
stories.summary: A monster El Niño is nearing its peak, deepening drought in many parts of the world. Coming as countries slash foreign aid and war chokes supplies of energy and fertilizer, the climate phenomenon could leave millions more people in vulnerable countries without enough to eat. Read more on E360 →

stories.body:
Dried up rice fields in West Java, Indonesia, where El Niño is fueling an extended drought. Ali Lutfi / NurPhoto via Getty Images

A monster El Niño is nearing its peak, deepening drought in many parts of the world. Coming as countries slash foreign aid and war chokes supplies of energy and fertilizer, the climate phenomenon could leave millions more people in vulnerable countries without enough to eat.

By Nicola Jones • November 5, 2026

Facebook

Twitter

LinkedIn

Email

The world is now in the grip of a super El Niño: a Godzilla-sized version of a natural climate phenomenon that has already shriveled rivers, upended aquaculture, and flattened crops with drought. But the global organizations that keep an eye on food security are warning of even tougher times ahead.

The impacts of an El Niño can be far reaching and catastrophic. In the late 19th century, one of the strongest El Niños on record helped to fuel multiyear droughts across Asia, Brazil, and Africa that spurred a global famine: Some 50 million people, or 3 percent of the global population, died. Thankfully, the ways we plan for bad weather and move food around the planet have improved massively since then, with organizations working hard to provide relief where it’s needed. But the impacts of bad weather on crops are still hard to avoid. After a strong El Niño hit in 2015, cereal yields across Southern Africa were 20 percent below normal; crop yields in parts of Ethiopia dropped by 90 percent.

This year’s El Niño has already, by one measure, topped those previous record holders in strength. And it’s still growing. By the time the phenomenon peaks in early winter, sea-surface warming in the tropical Pacific could be higher than anything seen in a millennium. In August, the World Food Programme warned that this El Niño might push an additional 49 million people into acute food insecurity by the end of 2027, taking the total number to 274 million. Worryingly, this year’s event comes as global aid dollars are pinched and wars are making it hard to plug holes in global food systems.

Global food prices have been trending upwards for 20 years, thanks to climate change. This year brings additional strains.

“It’s a triple whammy of high fertilizer costs, high energy costs, and now massive droughts across the tropics,” says Berkeley Earth climatologist Zeke Hausfather, who is watching the situation unfold. “It’s not a great story.” The El Niño is one phase of a natural climate pattern called the El Niño–Southern Oscillation, which has a dramatic impact on global rainfall patterns. El Niño years are marked by unusually warm waters in the tropical Pacific, which weaken winds across that patch and alter global patterns of rising and falling air pressure. The results are complicated and variable, but they tend to bring dry conditions to some tropical areas — including the Amazon and parts of Australia and Africa — and rain to other places, including Florida. The other side of the oscillation, La Niña, is marked by cooler ocean temperatures and a different pattern of wet and dry. The planet swings between the two in irregular intervals of years, sometimes with neutral periods in between.

Both sides of this cycle can harm crops, though one prominent 2014 study found that El Niño affects a larger swath of the globe’s harvested land. While some places get more water, and some crops thrive, in many spots drought withers production. That same study found that an El Niño tends to improve global soybean production by up to 5 percent but suppresses maize, rice, and wheat by up to 4 percent. The numbers in any one country can be much more dramatic than that: Since 1980, South Africa’s maize output, for example, has averaged about 28 percent below normal during El Niño years.

Children are treated for malnutrition in Ifotaka, Madagascar. Drought, fueled by El Niño, is expected to worsen food shortages. Razafindrakoto Mamy Nirina / AFP via Getty Images

Cereal disruptions, even if small, can hit hard if they come on top of other economic strains, says Stanford agricultural economist David Lobell. “When markets are tight, then if there’s a drought somewhere, that’s a much bigger deal.”

And the markets are, indeed, tight. Global average food prices have been trending upwards for about 20 years, says Lobell, thanks to climate blows stacking on top of each other. And this year has brought additional strains. When the U.S. and Israel launched an attack on Iran at the end of February, marine traffic through the Strait of Hormuz ground to a near halt for months. The transport of oil was choked, energy prices spiked, and the supply of fertilizer, which is most often made with hydrogen sourced from cheap natural gas, was severely pinched: The Middle East usually produces a quarter of the world’s fertilizer. Meanwhile, the ongoing war in Ukraine continues to play havoc with the cost of fuel and restrict the transport of wheat from a major hub on the Black Sea.

As of October, the warming in the mid-tropical Pacific that’s used to measure the strength of an El Niño hit 3.5 degrees C — breaking the previous record of about 2.75 degrees C — and is on its way to an unprecedented peak of around 4 degrees C, according to Hausfather. “That’s scary,” he says. Broadly speaking, he says, the more powerful the El Niño, the more powerful its effects on weather events, including droughts.

In northern Sudan, rainfall totals have been less than half of normal, which is expected to take a toll on both crops and livestock.

Unusually, this year’s El Niño is the third “strong” El Niño event to hit within a relatively short span of 11 years, which means some areas have been hit repeatedly with drought. The higher-than-usual frequency of El Niños may itself be caused by climate change, some researchers have suggested — though this is still an area of hot debate, Hausfather says.

All these factors act together, with cascading impacts that can take months to develop and last for years. “The confluence of drought and conflict drives some of the worst outcomes we see,” says Richard Choularton, director of climate and resilience for the World Food Programme in Rome. A farmer can’t afford fertilizer; then his fields face drought. In anticipation of a bad year, he plants less and hires fewer people. The river used to transport his crop dries up, and the port that takes it overseas has been bombed out of commission. His cows have little to eat. A year later, he can’t afford to buy groceries or fuel his farming equipment. The lack of rain allows seawater to seep into aquifers, so fresh water gets rationed. Hydropower plants sputter. And on it goes.

While any year brings its own spates of bad weather — some of it random, and some made more likely by the pressures of climate change — plenty of events this year have been attributed to the El Niño. Among the first to be hit was the Peruvian anchovy fishery, which was closed dramatically early this year to give anchovies a fighting chance in the face of warm waters and less plankton, one of their main food sources. This industry, typically worth between $2 billion and $3 billion, is a huge contributor to global feed for livestock and aquaculture. As of September, global fishmeal output was about half what it was the year before; fishmeal prices have spiked, with some European salmon farmers turning to cheaper chicken byproducts.

Farmer Darwin Cruz in Los Piches, Honduras, where animals are dying amid one of the worst droughts in decades. Orlando Sierra / AFP via Getty Images

In Indonesia, palm oil mills stopped buying fruit from farmers because an ongoing drought shriveled the area’s main transportation artery, the Kapuas River. In Cambodia, a delayed rainy season is drying out rice fields. Panama has declared a national state of emergency (as it did for the 2023 and 2015 El Niños), and the Panama Canal is carrying less ship traffic and transporting less food in the face of dwindling rainfall. In northern Sudan, rainfall totals have been less than half of normal, which is expected to take a toll on both crops and livestock from March to August next year. El Niño-induced drought alongside record summer temperatures in Central America has eaten away at crop yields and threatens that region’s second planting cycle: The E.U.’s Joint Research Centre projects an 83 percent spike in people suffering from acute food insecurity in that area.

Perhaps surprisingly, the global food production outlook for this growing season isn’t as bad as one might think: The Famine Early Warning Systems Network (FEWS NET) notes that the USDA projects worldwide production of maize, wheat, and rice for 2026-2027 to be just 2.7 percent below the previous year’s production, which will still make it the second largest annual crop on record. “Globally, food supply is not of high concern,” says FEWS NET advisor Amy Ostrander. “The concerns are production changes in some specific regions, such as Southern Africa, and food access.” Even if sufficient crops are harvested in those regions, in other words, some food won’t make it to market and some people won’t be able to afford it.

An analysis by the United Nations Food and Agriculture Organization concludes that the highest risks from El Niño-prompted droughts will be in the Sahel, Southern Africa, South and Southeast Asia, and in Central America’s Dry Corridor and the Caribbean.

While 2026 is warm, “2027 is going to be the record-shattering year,” says a climate scientist.

One good thing about an El Niño is that meteorologists can see it coming almost a year in advance, unlike freak weather events, which are harder to forecast. This gives agencies a fighting chance to protect people by distributing drought-resistant seeds, for example, securing deals for future emergency food supplies and transport, or setting up income assistance for struggling farmers.

The World Food Programme first tested its forecast-based financing program in Zimbabwe during the 2015 El Niño: Delivering cash to families in one district facing drought helped them to sustain their quantity and quality of food, while a neighboring district that didn’t receive cash aid saw a massive drop. This year, the WFP has been delivering cash and other assistance, including, for example, more than 3,000 airtight silos for farmers in Guatemala to help them safely store grain. As of October, the program says it has reached 28 million people across 15 countries with early warning information and assistance.

Cash is strapped for such programs, though. Funds for global aid were down 30 percent in 2025 from their 2022 peak and are still falling, making it hard for the WFP and others to do their work. In Somalia, the WFP helped 10 million people during a drought in 2022; today, in the face of similar conditions, says Choularton, they can afford to reach less than a million.

El Niño is fueling both droughts and floods, leaving vulnerable countries at risk of food shortages. Sources: Food and Agriculture Organization / World Food Programme / Columbia Climate School. Yale Environment 360 / Made with Flourish

Advanced warning is good, says Lobell, but challenges will still abound, and even harder times may lie ahead as El Niños pile on top of climate change. The peaks of strong El Niños are almost always followed by record-breaking years for the global average temperature. The anomalously hot years of 1998, 2016, and 2024 (the current record holder) all followed hot on the heels of El Niño peaks the year before. While 2026 is warm, “2027 is going to be the record-shattering year,” says Hausfather.

Global warming, of course, also has impacts on food supply. Last year, Lobell published a paper showing that total wheat, barley, maize, rice, and soybean yields are now altogether about 5 percent lower overall than they would have been in a world without climate change. “To a lot of people that sounds like a small number. But the kind of shocks that we talk about can be far smaller than that,” he says. “It doesn’t take much of a supply shift to have an important effect on people’s lives.”

Because the specific places that get warmer and drier during El Niños are different from the specific places that get warmer and drier from climate change, researchers caution that what we see in 2026 won’t be a precise forerunner of things to come. But how we deal with this temporary challenge does say something about the resilience of our food systems, says Lobell, and it will reveal how we might cope in the future with other climate disruptions to crops. “That’s one of the big questions,” he says. “How much can you adapt when the conditions are bad?”
