stories.body:
The ambition of the 21st century should no longer be to maximize growth, but to maximize prosperity.

Philipp Humm is an artist, author and ex-tech CEO living in Milan.

More than 2,000 years ago, Aristotle formulated one of history’s most remarkable thought experiments. What, he asked, would happen if tools could obey commands, even anticipate them? What would happen if they could carry out their work entirely on their own?

“If every instrument could accomplish its own work, obeying or anticipating the will of others,” he wrote in “Politics” around 350 B.C.E., “if the shuttle would weave and the plectrum touch the lyre without a hand to guide them, chief workmen would not need servants, nor masters slaves.”

For centuries, this passage was understood primarily as a philosophical allegory. Today, what is striking is not Aristotle’s technical imagination but his political imagination. He was more interested in the social consequences of self-operating machines than in their feasibility.

Artificial intelligence forces us to confront this issue anew: What becomes of a society whose economy, purpose and welfare state are built on wage labor if wage labor loses that foundational role? Perhaps the true AI revolution will begin in our conception of what it means to be human, not inside Silicon Valley’s data centers.

More Or Less?

What’s better: more people or less work for humans? Few contradictions capture our historical moment more precisely. Never before has a society simultaneously spent so much money attempting to compensate for labor shortages while investing so much in technologies designed to eliminate labor altogether.

If current fertility rates continue and net migration falls to zero, United Nations projections suggest that many Western populations will shrink by about 30% by the end of this century. In countries such as Italy, the decline approaches 40%-50%. Governments have responded with generous family subsidies and large-scale immigration programs but have seen limited economic success. Research suggests that immigration’s fiscal contribution depends heavily on education, employment, age at arrival and migration motive. Highly skilled migrants, the minority, tend to generate net economic gains, whereas low-skilled immigration, the majority, can impose a net fiscal drag on advanced welfare states.

In Britain, falling fertility, population aging and migration have become inseparable topics. Parliamentary debates frequently frame birth rates as a long-term growth problem. At the same time, the government seeks to reduce reliance on migrant labor by expanding domestic training programs. In the United States, similar arguments are made from the opposite side: Economists warn that the native-born labor force is shrinking and that immigration now supplies much of America’s labor-force growth. Also, a new Silicon Valley pronatalism has emerged. Elon Musk, Peter Thiel and other technology leaders warn that collapsing birth rates threaten civilization, even as their companies build systems designed to reduce the economy’s dependence on human labor.

In addition to trying to stabilize the size of their labor force, governments invest aggressively in artificial intelligence to stay internationally competitive. The labor displacement that these technologies will ultimately produce is often ignored or dismissed with reassuring promises that new jobs will inevitably emerge, as they always have in the past.

“Perhaps the true AI revolution will begin in our conception of what it means to be human.”

The management of this contradiction is even more striking in East Asia.

South Korea, with a fertility rate of around 0.75 children per woman, is experiencing a demographic collapse unprecedented in peacetime. The government spends tens of billions each year on birth and family incentives and housing programs designed to reverse the trend. So far, little success. Simultaneously, South Korea has become the most robot-intensive economy in the world with over 1,000 industrial robots per 10,000 manufacturing workers.

Japan presents a similar picture. Its working-age population has been declining for more than two decades, and the country has responded by pursuing one of the world’s most ambitious automation and robotics strategies. Today, Japan possesses one of the highest densities of industrial robots with more than 400 per 10,000 manufacturing workers, compared to the world average of around 120-150.

South Korea and Japan offer a preview of the intelligence economy. Their governments are investing in automation to compensate for shrinking workforces while trying to arrest population decline to preserve domestic demand and the fiscal foundations of their welfare states. Both policies make sense within the industrial economy. But what happens when AI and robotics reduce the economy’s dependence on human labor? Could demographic decline and automation eventually become complementary rather than opposing forces?

The Invention Of Homo Faber

The labor society as we know it today is not an anthropological constant. For most of human history, people were not primarily Homo faber — the productive individual who derives social worth from economic work. They became so only with the rise of modernity, and above all through the Industrial Revolution.

In classical antiquity and most of medieval Europe, manual labor was regarded as a necessity performed largely by slaves and the lower classes. The privileged classes devoted themselves to politics, philosophy, religion, war, arts and leisure. As Hannah Arendt observed in “The Human Condition” (1958), modernity radically overturned the classical hierarchy of human activities. Labor, once regarded as a necessity of life rather than its purpose, increasingly became the organizing principle of society.

Adam Smith provided the intellectual economic foundation for this transformation. In “The Wealth of Nations” (1776), he argued that the true wealth of a nation lies in the total productive labor of its people, not in gold, land or trade surpluses.

Around 1800, roughly 75% of Americans worked in agriculture. Today, fewer than 2% do. America’s industrial transformation created an entirely new economic logic, one symbolized by Henry Ford’s famous wage increase in 1914. Ford understood that his workers should build automobiles and earn enough to buy them. That insight captured the genius of industrial capitalism: production, wages and demand were bound together.

“If artificial intelligence assumes an increasing share of productive labor, society will have to find answers to how to cultivate lives that remain meaningful outside employment.”

This model was at the core of Western democracies throughout the 20th century. Wages financed taxation, welfare systems and pensions. At the same time, they generated income that sustained consumption and served as the principal mechanism of social integration. In numbers, labor accounts for up to 60% of GDP and private consumption for nearly 70% for OECD nations.

The importance of wages extends far beyond the hours people spend at work. Every productive hour finances about nine hours of non-working life: the years of childhood, education and retirement; evenings, weekends and illnesses. Another way to look at it is that every hour of paid work supports those hours of non-working life across society, including workers’ own time outside employment and that of children, students, retirees, homemakers and other dependents. Historically, these ratios have increased, driven mainly by reductions in working hours and increases in life expectancies.

When jobs become scarcer or wages lose their economic bargaining power, this architecture begins to fracture. This puts immense pressure on public finances: Children, retirees, students, the sick and much of public spending ultimately depend on the wages of the working population.

The defining economic problem of our century so far has been How does a society finance ever more years of life with ever fewer years of work? For decades, advanced economies have managed to answer that question through a fragile combination of economic growth and rising public debt. But what happens when artificial intelligence begins to undermine the labor market on which that answer rests?

When Intelligence Becomes Cheap

Every major technological revolution transformed a scarce factor of production into an abundant one. The Industrial Revolution dramatically reduced the cost of mechanical energy with fossil fuels. Globalization in the 1990s and 2000s lowered the cost of physical labor by integrating China and other emerging economies into global production networks. The AI revolution may now do the same with intelligence. Cognition, coordination, pattern recognition and many forms of decision-making could become abundant rather than scarce resources.

John Maynard Keynes anticipated this possibility almost a century ago. In his 1930 essay “Economic Possibilities for our Grandchildren,” he warned of what he called technological unemployment: the possibility that humanity might discover ways of saving labor faster than it could discover new uses for it.

For decades, economists largely dismissed this concern in two ways. The first was Joseph Schumpeter’s theory of creative destruction. Technological progress destroys existing occupations, but it also creates new industries, new professions and ultimately more productive forms of employment. The second was historical experience. Every previous technological revolution had ultimately generated more people employed, not mass unemployment.

With AI, this historical adjustment mechanism may no longer be applicable.

The Stanford economist Erik Brynjolfsson has described this possibility as the “Turing Trap.” Previous generations of machines primarily replaced physical labor in a few defined routines. Human beings remained one step above the machines, becoming their planners or problem-solvers. That historical shock absorber is now shrinking. AI is increasingly performing many of the cognitive activities that once enabled workers to move up the value chain.

MIT’s Daron Acemoglu arrived at a similar conclusion from a different direction. He argues that the key issue is how firms choose to deploy AI. If businesses use AI primarily to replace workers rather than to augment their productivity, the historical pattern of technological progress creating more employment than it destroys might no longer hold. The structure of the emerging AI economy already reflects this logic. Many of today’s most valuable AI companies generate extraordinary market value with remarkably small workforces.

Agentic AI further accelerates this process. Agents no longer automate isolated tasks; they increasingly perform entire workflows: analyzing information, correcting errors, adapting strategies and coordinating complex processes with minimal human intervention.

“For the first time since the Industrial Revolution, labor could cease to be the economy’s scarcest factor of production.”

For companies, the decisive issue is simple: Can AI perform economically valuable tasks at substantially lower cost than humans? Increasingly, for many roles, the answer is yes.

The substitution of labor by machines is unfolding in two waves.

The first affects white-collar work. A junior financial analyst, lawyer, management consultant or software engineer in London or New York may cost an employer 80-100 per hour. Modern language models can already perform many of their tasks for a fraction of a cent. Systems possess another structural advantage. While the knowledge accumulated by an employee spreads only gradually through an organization and often disappears when that employee leaves, improvements made by software are retained and deployed instantly and at scale across an entire system.

The second wave is now reaching the physical economy and the blue-collar population. Humanoid robots developed by companies such as Tesla and China’s Unitree are learning increasingly complex movements through observation and simulation. Their manufacturers hope eventually to reduce operating costs to below $2 per hour. This is in stark contrast to 30-50 per hour for an average American worker.

Research by the International Monetary Fund suggests that nearly 60% of jobs in advanced economies will be affected by artificial intelligence, with almost half facing substantial disruption or substitution. Against that background, a reduction of roughly 30% in total employment over the coming decades no longer appears implausible. Whether the final figure is 20% or 40% is ultimately of secondary importance.

What matters is that, for the first time since the Industrial Revolution, labor could cease to be the economy’s scarcest factor of production. If that is true, the consequences extend far beyond the labor market. They force us to reconsider one of the deepest assumptions of the industrial age.

Shrinking Rich

It is precisely at this point that a possibility emerges that remains almost unthinkable in the discourse today: Population decline, discussed almost exclusively as an economic catastrophe, may prove to be an essential corrective during the intelligence revolution. I call this the 30/30 equilibrium.

The idea is simple. Imagine an advanced economy whose population gradually declines by around 30% over several decades while artificial intelligence and robotics reduce labor demand by a similar magnitude. These developments will not occur simultaneously or at the same pace, yet over time they could broadly offset one another. Fewer people require fewer jobs. As a result, the historical ratio between productive labor and the total population could remain remarkably stable without placing an additional burden on public finances.

The 30/30 equilibrium is, first and foremost, a theory of macroeconomic stabilization in which demographic decline ceases to be an economic disaster and becomes part of the adjustment mechanism. However, it does not create prosperity.

Whether a shrinking society also becomes richer depends on a second variable: capital deepening. As the Solow-Swan growth model demonstrates, long-run prosperity depends less on the size of the labor force than on the amount and productivity of capital available to each worker. If AI and robotics increase productive capital faster than the labor force contracts, output per person continues to rise even while the total workforce declines. Read Noema in print.

If we want an economy’s GDP to stabilize, we need a booster. A 30% decline in the labor force would have to be offset by roughly a 45% increase in capital productivity. This would raise GDP per capita by more than 40%. Given the learning curves already observed in semiconductors, computing power, artificial intelligence and robotics, together with the widening cost advantage of machine intelligence over human labor, such productivity gains no longer appear particularly ambitious.

Now, suppose instead that the population remained constant while productive capital increased by the same 45%. Total output would then expand by roughly 20%. Conventional economics would celebrate this as the superior outcome.

William Stanley Jevons observed in the 19th century that more efficient steam engines did not reduce Britain’s coal consumption. They increased it. As energy became cheaper, new applications emerged, further expanding demand.

Efficiency produced abundance, but abundance also produced greater resource use. The same dynamic may now apply to intelligence. As AI becomes cheaper, we will almost certainly consume far more of it. This applies to cognitive work as well as to robotics. Silicon Valley celebrates this future as “abundance.” Yet abundance is not necessarily environmentally sustainable. Every additional product made and consumed at a fraction of today’s cost and price still consumes energy and leaves a negative ecological footprint. In addition, AI systems require substantial electricity, computing infrastructure, rare materials and manufactured hardware. Abundance comes at a high cost to the physical world.

“For the first time in history, we may be able to become fewer without becoming poorer. We may even become richer while placing a lighter burden on the natural world.”

From an environmental perspective, allowing the population to decline naturally while increasing prosperity per person may therefore represent a superior equilibrium. For the first time since the Industrial Revolution, the intelligence economy offers us the possibility of choosing such an equilibrium.

This requires abandoning two assumptions inherited from the industrial age.

The first is financial. Modern economies are organized around debt, money creation and asset valuations that all depend on continual expansion. Tomorrow’s economy must become larger than today’s because yesterday’s obligations must be repaid. A “shrinking-rich economy” may ultimately require a monetary and financial system that derives its stability less from ever-expanding debt than from the growing productivity of capital.

The second is geopolitical. “Big is beautiful” belonged to an era in which economic and military strength depended directly on scale. Larger populations meant more workers, more consumers, more inventors, larger armies, bigger markets and greater geopolitical influence. The intelligence economy changes that logic. Human intelligence is scarce, but artificial intelligence expands usable intelligence at an extraordinary pace and cost, making it an abundant resource. Furthermore, technologies such as autonomous drones increasingly erode the traditional military advantages of scale. The same is true for economic influence.

Ecology offers a useful framework. The ecologist Eugene Odum distinguished between pioneer and climax ecosystems. Young forests grow aggressively, consume resources and prioritize speed over sustainability. Mature forests grow little yet contain far greater biomass, complexity, stability and resilience than the pioneer systems from which they emerged.

Human civilization may not be fundamentally different. The fossil-fuel economy was humanity’s pioneer phase. Its success rested on expansion: more people, more energy, more production and more consumption. Artificial intelligence, combined with demographic decline, might allow advanced societies to enter a different stage of development. Technologies such as robotic recycling, AI-managed precision fermentation and closed material loops already point toward an economy capable of creating greater prosperity with fewer material inputs.

The resulting climax society would not be a society of sacrifice. It would be a society that has learned to distinguish growth from prosperity. For the first time in history, we may be able to become fewer without becoming poorer. We may even become richer while placing a lighter burden on the natural world.

The ambition of the 21st century should no longer be to maximize growth but to maximize prosperity: to shrink rich.

Who Inherits The Loom?

If the intelligence economy delivers the productivity gains its advocates expect, it will generate unprecedented wealth. This raises the central political question of the post-labor age: Who receives the surplus?

Under the existing economic order, the answer is clear. The gains will accrue primarily to the owners of capital, not to labor, as ownership determines who has a claim on output. If AI and robotics replace labor as the decisive productive force, then income will shift away from wages and toward those who own the machines, models, data centers, energy systems and platforms through which the new economy operates.

This creates a problem even for the capital owners. Henry Ford understood that workers were producers and consumers. They had to earn wages sufficient to buy the cars they manufactured. The same logic applies to the intelligence economy but in a more unstable form. If machines produce goods while human beings lose the wages with which to buy them, the demand side of the economy weakens. Even the most productive AI economy ultimately depends on customers who can afford to buy what it produces.

Silicon Valley’s preferred answer to this problem is universal basic income (UBI). The idea is simple. The state provides citizens with a minimum income funded through higher taxes, increased public debt or levies on automated production. In the short term, some form of income floor may well be necessary. It could stabilize demand as the population shrinks and cushion the social shock of technological displacement.

But as a permanent settlement, UBI risks becoming a pharmakon: remedy and poison at the same time.

If financed through public debt, UBI injects additional money and purchasing power into the economy without increasing the supply of productive assets, creating inflationary pressure that erodes part of AI’s productivity gains. If financed by taxing production, businesses will ultimately recover much of the additional cost through higher prices, with a similar effect. In both cases, a significant share of the productivity dividend is dissipated rather than translated into higher real living standards.

Economic history offers a warning. In 1795, English magistrates introduced the Speenhamland system, a wage supplement designed to protect rural workers from poverty. It was intended as relief. In practice, it subsidized employers who could continue paying low wages while the public purse made up the difference. It also entrenched the poor’s dependence on local authorities.

The analogy is not exact, but the lesson matters. Income support may ease the transition, but it is unlikely to provide a durable foundation for a post-labor economy.

“What kind of human beings do we wish to become?”

The challenge, therefore, is to distribute the productivity gains of the intelligence economy without eroding them. That requires a financing mechanism that is neither debt-financed nor production-tax-financed.

Here, Karl Marx becomes newly relevant, though perhaps not for the reasons usually assumed. In the “Grundrisse,” he imagined a future in which wealth would no longer depend primarily on immediate labor time, but on the technological appropriation of what he called the “general intellect”: the accumulated knowledge, science and cooperative intelligence of society. Marx’s most contemporary insight was his recognition that knowledge would become the decisive productive force.

Artificial intelligence gives this idea a literal technological form. AI models are not created in a vacuum. They are trained on the accumulated intellectual inheritance of humanity: books, scientific papers, Wikipedia entries, forum discussions, software libraries, images, public archives, open-source code and countless traces of human communication. They also depend on publicly funded research, energy infrastructure, universities, telecommunications networks, roads, water systems and legal protections. The intelligence economy is built by both private firms and a civilizational commons.

Therefore, should the returns from these systems accrue exclusively to private owners, or should society retain a claim on the productive infrastructure that emerged from its collective knowledge?

The 20th century solved the demand problem through wages. Silicon Valley proposes to solve it through transfers. The intelligence economy may ultimately solve it through ownership.

Society’s claim to a universal capital dividend, instead of a UBI, could take the form of ownership, where governments would secure equity stakes, public stakes or sovereign wealth claims in AI infrastructure that depends on public resources, public data and public markets to operate. The proceeds would not flow into general budgets but would instead be distributed directly to citizens as a universal dividend.

Ownership operates differently economically and is not inflationary. It distributes the productivity gains directly at their source, preserving the full efficiency gains of automation while broadening participation in the wealth it creates.

The former wage-earning seamstress would become a shareholder in the loom rather than a dependent of the state. Aristotle imagined a world in which the self-weaving loom abolished the necessity of labor. The intelligence economy gives us the opportunity to decide who inherits it.

The Devil In Paradise

Suppose we succeed. Imagine that artificial intelligence performs most productive labor, demographic decline cushions the adjustment, a new ownership model distributes the gains of automation without sacrificing productivity and advanced societies once again live within ecological limits. Humanity would come remarkably close to Aristotle’s vision of the self-weaving loom. We might finally become Homo curans.

Even then, two deeper challenges remain. The first concerns meaning. More than 70 years ago, Arendt warned of the danger of what she called “worldlessness.” A society organized around work does not automatically become a society of free citizens once work disappears. On the contrary, people might lose the shared public realm in which they experience responsibility, judgment and a sense of purpose. The deeper crisis of the post-labor age may therefore not be unemployment, but meaninglessness.

The anthropologist David Graeber reached a similar conclusion from a different direction. His analysis of “bullshit jobs” suggested that much contemporary employment does not survive because it is socially indispensable, but because modern societies have forgotten how to organize meaning outside paid work.

If artificial intelligence assumes an increasing share of productive labor, society will have to find answers to how to cultivate lives that remain meaningful outside employment.

The second challenge is even more far-reaching. As the world becomes more complex, we increasingly delegate decisions to artificial intelligence. At first, AI merely assists human judgment. Soon it recommends. Eventually, it decides. Every delegation begins as a convenience and may end in dependency. Human judgment gradually atrophies through disuse.

This process is already visible. We delegate navigation to algorithms, communication to recommendation systems, information retrieval to search engines, financial decisions to automated models, partner selection to matching applications and increasingly even legal and administrative decisions to AI-assisted systems. Each individual delegation appears rational. Together, they transform the relationship between human beings and judgment itself.

The logic of intelligent machines is not identical to the logic of human beings. Their purpose is optimization. Ours is judgment. Confusing the two may ultimately prove to be the deepest alignment problem of all.

As these systems increasingly surpass us in specialized domains, the risk is less that they become human than that humans gradually surrender their own capacity for judgment. We may discover too late that we have become second-class decision-makers in a world optimized by machines: Homo algorithmus.

More than 2,000 years ago, Aristotle asked what would happen if the shuttle could weave by itself. Today, that is a reality. But the self-weaving loom leaves us asking: What kind of human beings do we wish to become? Whether the intelligence economy gives rise to Homo curans or Homo algorithmus will not be decided by technology, but by us.

stories.title: Is the Far-Right Wave Receding?
stories.summary: But there is a deeper dissatisfaction with democracy that the far right continues to exploit. The post Is the Far-Right Wave Receding? appeared first on Foreign Policy In Focus .

stories.body:
Former President of Serbia Aleksandar Vucic and U.S. President Donald Trump (Anna Moneymaker-Pool/Getty Images)

Originally published in Hankyoreh .

The victory of incumbent Lula in the Brazilian presidential election was a surprise. The longtime leftist politician ran second in the first round behind far-right challenger Flavio Bolsonaro—the son of disgraced former leader Jair Bolsonaro—and no one in the history of Brazilian democracy had come from behind to win in the second round. But by mounting a huge get-out-the-vote effort, Lula defied all predictions.

Lula also defied the current trend in Latin American elections. In the last 18 months, right-wing candidates had won in seven countries, including Chile, Colombia, and Peru. The trend worldwide has been similar, with the far right winning in local elections in Germany, the extremist party of Marine Le Pen leading the polls in France, and the far right participating in governments in Italy, Finland, and the Czech Republic. Far right leaders remain in place in Russia, India, the Philippines, and, for now, Israel.

Is Lula the outlier? Or does he perhaps represent a political course correction?

For those eager to see a political wave in the making, Lula is not the only example of the electoral repudiation of the far right. On the same day as the Brazilian elections, students managed to oust the longtime autocrat Aleksandar Vucic in the equally surprising Serbian elections. Earlier this year, Viktor Orban also lost at the hands of a unified opposition. The massive “blue wave” rejection of Donald Trump in the midterm elections in the United States has continued the trend.

There is a natural feeling among voters in democratic societies to “throw the bums out.” In Latin America, a “pink” wave of progressive politicians like Ecuador’s Rafael Correa and Colombia’s Gustavo Petro has given way to a “brown” wave of ultra-conservative politicians. Voters, especially in today’s quicksilver environment of social media, respond positively to candidates who promise sweeping change. And thus, the political pendulum swings from left to right and back again.

But the far right is not just another conventional option on the political menu. It offers something radically different because it threatens to undermine the very democratic norms by which it has achieved power. In countries like Russia, Hungary, Turkey, and India, right-wing authoritarians have used democratic means—elections, constitutional changes, legal challenges—to weaken democracy. Other leaders have attempted to do away with democracy much more rapidly, as Jair Bolsonaro tried to do when he plotted to overturn the Brazilian elections that Lula won four years ago. Inspired by these rule-breakers, even traditional conservative politicians, like Yoon Suk Yeol in Korea, have attempted to suspend democracy.

And then there’s the case of Donald Trump. The U.S. president was reelected despite his efforts to overturn the 2020 elections that he lost. During his second term, he has attempted to unilaterally change the constitution. He has ignored court orders, bypassed Congress, and waged war against the mainstream media. He has repeatedly called into question the legitimacy of elections.

But Trump now has the lowest approval rating— 31 percent —of his presidency. In the midterm elections, voters rejected Trump’s party. The Democratic Party has easily retaken control of the House of Representatives, and it now has a comfortable margin of control in the Senate as well.

Unlike in Brazil, American voters are prioritizing their pocketbooks. A narrow majority of Brazilians supported Lula despite the country’s problems with debt and inflation. American voters, on the other hand, are abandoning Trump because of the economy—rising gas prices, the impact of sanctions, the consequences of the Iran War. As they demonstrated by electing Trump to a second term, many American voters don’t seem concerned about his anti-democratic rhetoric or actions.

This, more than the specific victories of the far right, is the more distressing takeaway. After all, democracy is not exactly enjoying its finest hour at the moment. Global freedom, according to the latest Freedom House report, declined for the twentieth consecutive year last year, with the United States, Bulgaria, Italy, El Salvador, and Madagascar registering significant deterioration in political and civil liberties.

Voters are turning toward anti-democratic candidates in part because they are disenchanted with democracy itself. Democratic mechanisms just don’t seem up to the task of addressing the threats currently facing the globe. Democracies have proved incapable of slowing climate change or responsibly controlling technologies like AI. Democracies have utterly failed at ensuring broad prosperity in a globalizing economy. If democrats were more successful at dealing with these problems, the far right’s promises of top-down solutions and returning to mythic pasts would not be so appealing.

This deeper problem with democracy suggests that even if the far right loses elections—in Brazil last month, the United States this week, France next year—it will not gracefully surrender the stage. Figures like Yoon Suk Yeol and Jair Bolsonaro can be jailed for their transgressions—and perhaps Trump too will follow in their footsteps. But voters will keep turning to more authoritarian alternatives if democratic institutions don’t deliver and democratic values don’t appeal.

The far right does not offer any better answers to the world’s problems. Its general response to global threats has been to turn its back. The far right supports high tariff walls, more fossil fuel extraction, and stricter controls on immigration. It repudiates all forms of globalization, lumping together neoliberal trade policies with Green energy programs and sensible approaches to immigration. The far right despises democracy not just because it puts controls on autocratic leaders but because of its association with globalization.

This, then, is the essential task of both the left and the center—to devise a new, robust internationalism that provides concrete gains to the average person while also safeguarding the planet for the next generations.

Until this happens, far-right candidates will continue to win. They might lose this or that election. But they will continue to win support with their anti-global agenda, while remaining focused on their ultimate goal of destroying democracy. They don’t want to be subject to the pendulum swings of democratic politics. They want to rip out the pendulum so that they can remain in power indefinitely.

stories.body:
My friend was due to be released next January. Under draconian security laws, his sentence has been extended by 10 years

T wo years ago, I wrote in this newspaper about the lengthy imprisonment of my friend Joshua Wong, who I spent years campaigning alongside for the advancement of Hong Kong’s democracy. He was given an unjust sentence meant to keep him behind bars until January 2027. He was supposed to be released in a few months, when I hoped he would finally be able to reunite with his friends and family and embark on a new chapter.

But this hope was misplaced. The end of the tunnel isn’t next year; it’s late 2036. By then, he will be 40. On Thursday, Joshua was sentenced to another 10 years under Hong Kong’s national security law for colluding with foreign forces. He is the only political prisoner who’s been convicted twice under the national security law. The judge described Joshua and me as “two ringleaders or masterminds” urging foreign powers to impose sanctions and other hostile actions against the Chinese and Hong Kong governments. The judgment cited previous international advocacy work, media interviews, social media posts and the political activities of Demosistō, the youth-led democratic party we founded.

Much of the cited evidence predates the implementation of the national security law, even though the court insisted it was not being applied retrospectively. Before 2020, meeting with foreign parliamentarians, engaging with and speaking to international institutions, and advocating for measures against human rights abuses were ordinary campaign strategies. These were peaceful means through which we tried to hold those in power accountable. The campaigns raised the profile of Hong Kong’s protests and garnered substantial support; they were so effective that Beijing had to impose the national security law to curb them and impose extensive legal punishments.

There is a stark lack of evidence about Joshua’s actions. Prosecutors said that he conspired with campaigners including myself to ask foreign bodies to impose sanctions on China – relying on his sharing of Facebook posts written by me. But these posts did not directly call for sanctions – they made other appeals, including for digital forensic companies to terminate their cooperation with the Hong Kong police. There’s no evidence that Wong himself advocated for imposing any form of sanctions, or that he had any direct link to advocacy work outside Hong Kong. The court also accepted that no organisation or funding supported his activities after the law came into force.

Still, as flimsy as the evidence is, it’s enough to secure him a decade in jail. The crux of the trial is not legal; it’s political. It is clear that Beijing exercises sweeping control over Hong Kong’s legal and political systems. This can be seen in the tightening of the electoral system by introducing an Iranian-style vetting mechanism , in the jailing of peaceful political dissidents and the emphasis placed on the necessity of “patriots ruling Hong Kong” .

When Chinese leaders categorise Jimmy Lai, Benny Tai and Joshua Wong as the “masterminds” behind the 2019 pro-democracy protests, the legal system must deliver sentences that reflect the trio’s “importance” . That’s why Lai and Tai have been sentenced to 20 years and 10 years respectively, and rank among the most persecuted pro-democracy figures in the region. There are now close to 2,000 political prisoners in Hong Kong.

It’s devastating that Joshua has been behind bars for such a large portion of his adult life. I couldn’t even imagine skipping 16 years before I reached my 40s – during which time many people meet their partner, get married, raise a family and settle into a career. Joshua has been deprived of living fully because of his advocacy for important democratic values. The sentence signals to the world that China is determined to quash any hopes for freedom and democracy on its soil.

As geopolitical competition intensifies and populism rises, human rights are increasingly treated as an inconvenience to diplomatic and economic interests. Governments speak of stability and pragmatic engagement, while political prisoners slowly disappear from international public attention. The Chinese regime has little reason to change its approach if the repression of Hong Kong carries no meaningful consequences, either to trade or its global standing.

Given that Hong Kong was a British colony until as recently as 1997, the UK, in particular, should not regard the territory as merely another foreign policy issue. The Sino-British joint declaration was intended to safeguard the city’s rights and freedoms. The British government should therefore make the release of Joshua, Jimmy Lai and other political prisoners a priority when dealing with Beijing, rather than responding to each new sentence with another ineffective statement of concern.

For months, I had imagined the day Joshua would finally be free. Now that hope has been pushed away for another decade. We must not forget him, and must take urgent action to demand his immediate release.

Nathan Law is a pro-democracy activist and former legislator from Hong Kong. He is a political refugee in the UK

Regulator’s initial ruling says algorithm ‘can be harmful’ and led young and vulnerable viewers ‘down rabbit holes they can’t easily escape’

TikTok has been charged by the European Commission with failing to protect users’ mental health by exposing them to a relentless stream of content that risks worsening eating disorders and anxiety in a case that strikes at its business model.

Issuing a preliminary ruling on Friday, the EU regulator said TikTok’s algorithm “can be harmful” and was leading young and vulnerable users “down rabbit holes they cannot easily escape from”.

The Chinese-owned short-video platform, which has 189 million users in the EU, was found to have failed to prevent users from being served up repetitive content on themes such as body image or isolation, which can lead to anxiety, sadness, worsen existing eating disorders or mental health problems.

Officials said their investigation focused on legal content, where a single video might not be problematic, but the cumulative effect of watching scores of them on one theme could damage users’ mental health.

TikTok’s safeguards to mitigate the risks of “rabbit-hole effects” – where users are served narrow and repetitive content to keep them engaged – were found to be ineffective. For example, officials said, if a user checked a “not interested” button on a video about eating patterns, the algorithm would still offer them similar content on diet and body image. Similarly, refreshing a feed only provided a brief respite from a stream of content on one topic, it found.

“Every time a user scrolls or likes a video on TikTok, the algorithm serves more of the same leading users down rabbit holes they cannot easily escape from,” said the European Commission’s lead official on tech policy, Henna Virkkunen. “TikTok needs to step up its efforts to protect users’ wellbeing, including those of minors.”

In response, a TikTok spokesperson said: “The commission has made a series of statements that are fundamentally inaccurate and distort our platform’s architecture and our commitment to user safety.

“We have a strong record of protecting our community while giving users direct and intuitive control over their content experience.”

The company argues that its policies prohibit content that promotes disordered eating and risky weight-management behaviours. It also says that more than 79 million users in the EU used its “not interested” or keyword filters to screen out unwanted content in the first six months of 2026.

The Molly Rose Foundation, which was set up in memory of 14-year-old Molly Russell, who took her own life in 2017 after being exposed to a torrent of harmful online content , welcomed what it called the landmark findings “to seek to hold TikTok to account for the way their algorithm drives young people down rabbit holes of despair”.

A survey for the charity earlier this year found that nearly half of girls and a third of all UK teenagers saw suicide, self-harm and eating-disorder content on social media in a week.

The foundation called on the UK regulator, Ofcom, to open an investigation into TikTok’s “extremely damaging” algorithm.

The EU investigation strikes at TikTok’s business model, which is built on keeping users scrolling as long as possible.

EU officials want TikTok to change the design of its ForYou feed, to give users greater control over the content they see.

“We are addressing a business model,” a commission official told reporters, saying that a business model focused mainly on engagement “can potentially create a risk” especially for minors and vulnerable adults.

The findings are part of a broader investigation launched in February 2024 under the Digital Services Act, which obliges large internet companies to take action to prevent a wide range of harms, from disinformation to damage to mental health.

The commission has already found the company violated EU rules over its “addictive design” for features such as infinite scroll. The company said at the time “the commission’s preliminary findings present a categorically false and entirely meritless depiction of our platform” and that it would challenge the findings.

A complaint about lack of transparency over who paid for TikTok’s advertising was resolved when the company made binding commitments to change its policies last December.

TikTok, which now has a chance to examine the investigation file and mount a defence, could agree to change its recommender system to avoid a fine.

If EU officials uphold the finding, the company could be fined up to 6% of its global worldwide turnover.

stories.title: Raise the Red Lantern review – Gong Li gives a decade-defining performance in an addictively ruthless masterpiece
stories.summary: Gong simmers with rage, loneliness and humiliation as the ‘fourth mistress’ navigating the intimate political savagery of her husband’s compound in Zhang Yimou’s 1991 drama Revisiting Zhang Yimou’s grippingly addictive psychological drama from 1991, adapted from a novella by Su Tong , is a reminder of what a great impact this movie made on western audiences. They responded to its arguably westernised tale of a young woman’s desperate loneliness in a sinister environment that resembles something by Charlotte Brontë or Daphne du Maurier. Like Jung Chang’s memoir Wild Swans from the same year, Raise the Red Lantern opened our eyes to 20th-century China’s secret theatre of cruelty and misogyny; elaborate domestic rituals of submission and servitude coexisted with infinitely subtle plotting, resentful manoeuvring and covert denunciation, habits of thought that could so easily be absorbed into Maoism. Gong Li gives one of the great performances of the 1990s as Songlian, a beautiful, intelligent young woman in 1920s China who is forced to abandon her university studies after just six months because her father has died and there is no longer money for the fees. In the unforgettable opening scene, which unfolds with a single unbroken shot of Gong’s pale face, incandescent with shock and pain, Songlian announces to her callous stepmother (who remains off camera) that she is ready to accept marriage – and then her eyes brim with tears. Her suppressed rage, loneliness and humiliation are to simmer below the surface for the rest of the film. Continue reading...

Gong simmers with rage, loneliness and humiliation as the ‘fourth mistress’ navigating the intimate political savagery of her husband’s compound in Zhang Yimou’s 1991 drama

R evisiting Zhang Yimou’s grippingly addictive psychological drama from 1991, adapted from a novella by Su Tong , is a reminder of what a great impact this movie made on western audiences. They responded to its arguably westernised tale of a young woman’s desperate loneliness in a sinister environment that resembles something by Charlotte Brontë or Daphne du Maurier. Like Jung Chang’s memoir Wild Swans from the same year, Raise the Red Lantern opened our eyes to 20th-century China’s secret theatre of cruelty and misogyny; elaborate domestic rituals of submission and servitude coexisted with infinitely subtle plotting, resentful manoeuvring and covert denunciation, habits of thought that could so easily be absorbed into Maoism.

Gong Li gives one of the great performances of the 1990s as Songlian, a beautiful, intelligent young woman in 1920s China who is forced to abandon her university studies after just six months because her father has died and there is no longer money for the fees. In the unforgettable opening scene, which unfolds with a single unbroken shot of Gong’s pale face, incandescent with shock and pain, Songlian announces to her callous stepmother (who remains off camera) that she is ready to accept marriage – and then her eyes brim with tears. Her suppressed rage, loneliness and humiliation are to simmer below the surface for the rest of the film.

Songlian arrives at the family compound of her autocratic new husband, Chen (Ma Jingwu), whose face is never clearly seen. This is virtually a walled city-state, subject to Chen’s implacably observed family traditions; Songlian is to be the “fourth mistress” occupying her own quarters, attended to by her own maidservant, the disobedient Yan’er (Kong Lin) who had hoped for “mistress” status herself. There are three other women, each in their own apartment: the stately, impassive “first mistress” Yuru (Jin Shuyuan) of Chen’s own age who has given him a grownup son; the homely, blandly smiling “second mistress” Zhuoyun (Cao Cuifen) who has only managed to give Chen a daughter; and the glamorous, haughty “third mistress” Meishan (He Saifei), a former opera singer who clearly resents Songlian, the new favourite.

Chen presides over it all like a Renaissance Tudor monarch, perhaps deriving unspoken erotic pleasure from capriciously transferring his attentions from one woman to the next. He has a bizarre tradition of putting red lanterns around the apartment of whichever of his mistress-wives he wishes to spend the night with, a decision that is bellowingly announced with elaborate formality by his major domo. (The “first mistress” never gets a red lantern, a mortification she accepts without comment.) And furthermore, the mistress currently enjoying Chen’s favour is allowed a privileged kind of foot-massage from a skilled ancient servant, a kind of quasi-conjugal pleasure.

In this way, Chen’s power and authority are imposed with a mesmeric choreography. For their part, his mistresses have to judge how and by how much to undermine each other without getting into trouble, and also how much to submit or show rebellion to Chen himself. A pouting display of resentment might amuse or arouse the master but, pushed too far, it might result in punishment and a disastrous loss of face. Poor Songlian is left alone for much of the day, and chances across a locked section of the compound where some unhappy mistresses are reputed to have died by hanging some time ago. She at first assumes that these women have taken their own lives, but as things turn out, this might not have exactly been the case. More and more, this dysfunctional household starts to resemble, in modern terms, a kind of death cult.

But it is Chen’s achievement – and in its way, the film’s achievement – to make you accept the normality of what is happening. The deeply strange business with the red lanterns and the foot massage is the culture of this enclosed world, which Songlian and the camera never leave. Songlian is to discover a plot against her, via the slippery and treacherous Yan’er who, as the lower-caste figure, is to pay a higher price than any of them. But the film shows that there are, potentially at any rate, any number of poisonous plots and stratagems swirling around at any moment. Survival is about anticipating them and turning them against one’s enemies without abandoning the mask of sisterly politeness.

This is a thrilling, fascinating study in intimate political savagery and a ruthless competition for the right to exist. The women are pitted against each other and their tragedy is that they do not realise that there is no difference between them; they are all decorative items, preserved, cherished or snuffed out like the red lanterns themselves.

In 2014 Burnham posted a supportive message on social media when Brand was facing media criticism about his housing arrangements

Published 6 November 2026

Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said Russell Brand has rightly been held to account for his "horrific" crimes and sought to explain Labour's previous association with the comedian.

Some within the Labour Party attempted to court Brand's support more than a decade ago, before police began investigating him - and in 2014 Burnham posted a supportive message on social media when the comedian was facing media criticism about his housing arrangements.

Asked about the 2014 tweet on Friday, Burnham said: "It's not always the case that people know everything about people in public life."

Brand was found guilty of one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault on Thursday.

In 2014, Brand was writing regular opinion pieces for newspapers and appearing on political discussion programmes, including the BBC's Question Time.

His anti-establishment and left-wing views had also gained him a following on social media.

The same year, Burnham, then the shadow health secretary, posted on Twitter in support of Brand following allegations about the comedian's housing arrangements.

It is not clear what Burnham had been referring to in his 2014 tweet, but the previous day, The Sun claimed Brand had paid rent at a property owned by a landlord in a tax haven, while at the same time campaigning against tax avoidance.

Brand threatened to sue the newspaper and said he would give the money to victims of the Hillsborough disaster, a group Burnham has long campaigned for.

At the time, Burnham said it was "depressing to see media mission to discredit someone who stops playing their game" and urged Brand to "keep going".

Asked about that social media post on Friday, Burnham told the BBC "all I can say is I had no idea of the full extent of what he was doing or what he went on to do".

The PM added: "His [Brand's] crimes are horrific, he's rightly been held to account, justice for the victims and that is the right course that's been taken here.

"It's not always the case that people know everything about people in public life, but what is important is that where there is wrongdoing it is exposed."

The prime minister added: "Credit to the victims, huge credit, the courage that it's taken, but also the journalists who've exposed this."

Ed Miliband, then the Labour leader, was interviewed by Brand in the run-up to the 2015 general election.

Brand, who had previously dismissed the idea of voting, backed Labour following the interview, saying Miliband had convinced him that "this bloke will listen to us".

Miliband, who is now foreign secretary, has previously said he regrets being interviewed by Brand .

On Friday, a spokesman for Miliband told the BBC: "These are horrific crimes that Russell Brand has been found guilty of and Ed's profound sympathy is with the victims.

"As he said in 2023, 'of course, knowing what I know now - and I was not aware of these allegations at the time about Russell Brand - I wouldn't have done that interview and I regret doing it'."

Brand was found not guilty of two other counts of rape, and one count of attempted indecent assault.

During a four-week trial, Brand faced allegations from six women spanning the decade between 1999 and 2009.

The 51-year-old was refused bail and will spend the weekend in custody before he is due to return to court on Monday for sentencing.

stories.title: Policing needs reform to cope with modern criminals, Met Police chief warns
stories.summary: The Met Police chief used a speech to argue that the current policing system in England and Wales is "heading for failure" without urgent change.

Watch: 'Degradation of policing' by not reforming force, says Met chief

Published 6 November 2026

The police system in England and Wales cannot cope against sophisticated modern criminals without urgent reform, the head of the Metropolitan Police has said.

In a speech on Friday, Sir Mark Rowley argued the system was "heading for failure" without change.

He is proposing eight to 10 regional police forces, supported by hundreds of local policing commands and a new national force, in what would be the biggest overhaul of policing since the 1960s.

The changes would replace the 43-force structure with three tiers: local teams dealing with neighbourhood issues, regional forces sharing specialist resources and a National Police Service tackling the most serious crimes.

In January it seemed that the many senior police officers were in favour of creating a National Police Service, and that organising into much larger regional forces had won the argument.

Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood produced a white paper that aligned with their ideas and asked the former Metropolitan Police Commissioner Lord Hogan-Howe to look at what the force boundaries might be.

But everything changed in July when Andy Burnham became prime minister. So far, Burnham has not spoken publicly about the plans, and the police chiefs are nervous that they may not have his backing. That may be why they have come out so strongly today, warning of the potentially apocalyptic effect of doing nothing.

As well as pushing hard for large regional forces, they are also making an argument about money which is familiar from the defence funding argument .

Sir Mark also pointed out that police funding in England and Wales has fallen from 0.9% of GDP to 0.7%. Implicit in that is that while the slice of the cake being allocated to defending the country is growing, the slice being allocated to defending people's communities and their homes is getting smaller.

Labour wants to shake up the police - but will that solve 'everyday crime epidemic'? Published 24 January

Number of police forces to be cut in major shake-up Published 22 January

Court system under massive strain, warns Met chief Published 12 October

In his speech, Sir Mark said organised crime groups, fraud networks, cyber-criminals and those involved in online child abuse increasingly operate across regional and international borders, while police forces remain organised around local areas.

"The victim remains local but increasingly the threat does not," he said citing the example of children who are "groomed by predators on another continent".

He argued that the current system is struggling to keep pace with these threats, saying: "We have 43 overstretched forces trying to do too much, with too little."

Merging forces would reduce duplication and could free up thousands of roles to be redirected towards front line policing, he believes.

Speaking on BBC Breakfast prior to his speech, Sir Mark said crime had changed a lot over the years but the police was largely organised how it was 60 years ago.

"Obviously the world's moved on a long way in that time."

His proposals follow a consultation launched by Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood in January. This included plans for a National Police Service to tackle the most complex crimes and a possible merger of the 43 forces into fewer, larger forces.

However some rural police and crime commissioners have described the plans as "political manoeuvring" by larger forces to "load the dice in their favour".

Dorset Police and Crime Commissioner David Sidwick reiterated his strong opposition to proposals to merge the forces.

"My concern is simple. If funding is diverted away from frontline services in Dorset to establish new national structures, local communities could end up receiving less rather than more."

In addition, Kent's Conservative police and crime commissioner Matthew Scott said: "[Sir Mark believes] policing should suffer a decade of disruption, that local policing services should be cut back and made more remote, and that this can all be done without ever asking the public what they want from their local police force."

The Association of Police and Crime Commissioners (APCC) has also questioned whether merging forces is the best way to improve policing.

It said: "The case for modernisation and a National Police Service is clear. The case for reducing 43 forces to nine regional 'mega-forces' is not."

Outgoing Cheshire Chief Constable Mark Roberts also said a future policing model needs to be built in a way that retains the places that already work well so that they do not "get subsumed" and end up "scrabbling to try and get resource from some of the metropolitan areas"

"Bigger isn't always better - we see some high performing big forces, we see some poorer performing big forces.

"The aim is to raise everyone at least to the minimum standard of the best," Roberts said after Rowley's speech.

Asked on Breakfast what would happen if the reforms were not put in place, Sir Mark said: "the risk is failure".

"Failure means solving fewer crimes, less local presence, when you get exceptional incidents like a certain outbreak of disorder like we saw in Hampshire."

In September police clashed with anti-migrant protesters in Portsmouth when 120 migrants arrived in a single dinghy.

"Standing still looks like a degradation of policing day by day, struggling even more as criminals outpace policing because we're not organised to meet it," Sir Mark added.

A Home Office spokesperson defended the plans, saying: "Our current model of policing has not changed since the 1960s and is no longer fit for purpose."

Sir Mark has also highlighted the financial pressures facing policing, saying that spending on policing had fallen from about 0.9% of GDP to 0.7% since 2010, which he said was as "a big hit".

"We do need investment as well, but if you threw loads of money at the current system it's still not going to fix the fundamental problem, it's not designed to meet today's challenges," he told the BBC.

"Throwing money at the current system isn't going to work."

Sir Mark said in his speech that years of underinvestment has left forces relying on ageing technology, and officers are increasingly diverted from neighbourhood policing to deal with other demands, including mental health and social care.

He also pointed to falling police performance, saying positive outcomes nationally are now less than half the level they were 12 years ago, while public confidence has fallen by 9%.

Andy Burnham says it isn't fair if an employer 'holds all the cards'

Published 5 November 2026

Businesses should publish salaries in job adverts now, Prime Minister Andy Burnham is telling firms, rather than wait for a new law to come in that will force them to do so.

The government is planning to make pay details compulsory in adverts, with legislation on the issue being brought forward "as soon as possible".

It argues the change will help jobseekers, particularly those applying for their first job, and could help prevent pay discrimination. However, one industry group said setting pay was a complex process and regulating adverts was not always suitable.

It comes a week after the UK's equality watchdog said employees should legally be able to find out what their colleagues are earning .

Burnham said the current system felt "weighted against the applicant" and the changes were aimed at "tilting the scales back".

"It can be quite soul destroying for young people these days, applying for jobs when the salary is not listed but sometimes they're not getting a reply," he told the BBC.

The prime minister added that publishing salaries in adverts was also important for closing the gender pay gap.

He was also challenged over whether MPs should be disclosing salaries when advertising for staff in their offices.

A number of politicians are currently advertising for roles without giving an expected salary. , external

Burnham said: "It would apply completely to them too and the call I'm making today is, before the law changes do it voluntarily because it's the right thing to do."

Greater transparency

The Cabinet Office launched a consultation into pay and reducing discrimination in the summer, and the government said there had been "overwhelming support" for greater transparency, with 94% of respondents backing the move.

"Whether you're a young person starting out or a parent trying to support your family, you should know what a job pays before spending your time and effort applying for it," Burnham said.

The government said the move was part of attempts to reduce the nearly one million young people not in education, employment or training - or "Neet" - ahead of the final report of the Milburn Review into youth inactivity, which is due in the coming weeks.

Publishing salary details upfront could "expose unjustified differences in pay, give workers greater confidence to challenge discrimination and prevent disagreements over pay escalating into disputes".

The proposals are similar to measures being introduced in the European Union. , external

Employers in Europe will have to disclose the initial pay or range for new roles, which must either be included in a published job advert or shared before an interview.

According to data from UK jobs website Adzuna , external , 51% of the adverts on its site in September had salary information, but the proportion has been falling in recent years.

Adzuna co-founder Andrew Hunter said being open about pay "should be the norm, not the exception".

He added that employers who put a salary on a job advert "attract more applicants, and better-suited ones".

'More complicated'

Previous research from the CIPD , external , an industry body for human resources managers, has indicated that the public sector and charities are more likely to reveal pay information that private firms, while pay ranges were more common than specific salaries.

But it found not all employers were "fully transparent", with pay ranges sometimes wider than £10,000.

CIPD chief executive Neil Carberry said that while, in principle, giving salary details was "a good thing", in practice it was "more complicated".

"There isn't always a single fixed figure, and employers will want to set pay based on a candidate's skills, experience and potential."

Carberry added the process was complex, saying that drafting job adverts is "best left to good employer practice rather than government regulation".

The government has said it will set out further details on what information will be required and how the legislation will be enforced "in due course".

Conservative shadow business secretary Julia Lopez said: "At a time when employers are finding it harder and harder to take on staff, Labour have decided to make their lives even more difficult.

"It should be up to businesses to decide what information they advertise about job openings, and to decide how to attract the best applicants.

"As long as they are not being dishonest, misleading or discriminatory, it should not be a matter for the government."

Last week, the Equality and Human Rights Commission (EHRC), said publishing salaries in job adverts would be a "positive step".

It also said bosses should be required to respond to questionnaires about colleagues' pay to cut pay discrimination.

At present, employers do not have to respond to employee requests for salary information about their co-workers.

The EHRC also said employers should be prevented from asking about current salary when offering a job to stop a history of discrimination from continuing.

Employers in the UK are currently allowed to ask you how much you get paid in your current role, but applicants are under no obligation to tell them .

stories.title: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang summoned by Congress over Chinese espionage concerns
stories.summary: Lawmakers want answers about Jensen Huang’s ties to an alleged Chinese intelligence asset.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Lawmakers want answers about Jensen Huang’s ties to an alleged Chinese intelligence asset.

Top Republican lawmakers have asked Jensen Huang to appear before Congress to answer questions after it was reported that US intelligence officials believe Nvidia’s chief executive has been targeted by a Chinese spying operation.

The chairs of the House committees on China, foreign affairs, and intelligence wrote to Huang this week asking him to appear before a joint closed-door briefing for their committees on November 18.

“Recent reports raise significant national security concerns regarding the People’s Republic of China’s access to sensitive US technology and information,” representatives John Moolenaar, Brian Mast, and Rick Crawford wrote.

“The issue of PRC infiltration and access to cutting-edge US technology is core to the investigative work of our three committees this Congress. It is vital that Congress determines the extent to which US national security has been placed at risk,” the lawmakers added.

The New York Times last week wrote that US intelligence officials believed Huang had been the target of a Chinese spy operation. The concerns center on a Chinese woman named Alice Huang, an executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based cloud company that has bought billions of dollars of Nvidia’s chips.

Nvidia has rejected the claims and on Thursday would not say if Huang would appear before Congress. “Meetings with customers are part of a CEO’s job. Jensen talks with thousands of customer executives every year,” the company said.

“Our regional cloud customers receive ordinary business information—not sensitive Nvidia trade secrets—and zero information relevant to national security,” it added.

The lawmakers said they wanted Huang to discuss the security protocols Nvidia had in place to protect against “foreign adversary espionage.” The company said its chief executive had an “outstanding security team” that travels with him.

The New York Times said Huang had not received a “defensive briefing,” which the intelligence community usually, but not always, provides potential espionage targets to warn them about the activity.

Nvidia said it was confident that the US government would have let the company know if it thought a person was a threat to US industry and that it often receives updates from Washington about people of concern.

The US has previously scrutinized Megaspeed, founded in 2023 as a spin-off from a Chinese gaming company, for potential chip smuggling, although no charges followed.

Nvidia launched its own unannounced on-site inspections at Megaspeed in Singapore when it became aware of the US concerns, but the internal probe found no evidence of its chips being diverted into China, said people familiar with the matter.

The company’s supply chain has come under increasing scrutiny as US export controls have prompted increased smuggling of its chips. Earlier this year Wally Liaw, a co-founder of Supermicro, one of Nvidia’s key supply chain partners, was arrested in the US and charged with smuggling Nvidia chips into China. He denies any wrongdoing and has pleaded not guilty.

stories.body:
Base rate increases from 3.75% and Bank governor signals another rise in near future to combat rising inflation

Analysis: Interest rate rise in midst of cost of living crisis will leave many incredulous

The Bank of England has raised interest rates for the first time in three years and warned of another increase to combat inflationary pressure unleashed by the Iran war.

Eight members of the Bank’s monetary policy committee (MPC) voted for the rise, which takes the base rate from 3.75% to 4%. The ninth member, Catherine Mann, preferred a more dramatic half-point increase.

The Middle East conflict has pushed oil prices persistently above $100 a barrel in recent months, as hopes have evaporated of a deal that could reopen the strait of Hormuz .

As a result, the Bank now expects UK inflation to rise to 4.9% in the middle of next year – up from 3.2% in its last economic forecast in July. Inflation hit 3.5% in September , as measured on the consumer prices index.

The decision, which will hit mortgage borrowers, comes a week after John Healey used his first budget to promise “breathing space” for hard-pressed consumers. Echoing the Office for Budget Responsibility’s gloomy forecasts for living standards , the MPC expects real post-tax income to fall this year and next.

The Bank’s governor, Andrew Bailey , raised the prospect of another rate rise in the near future – with a resolution to the Iran conflict the key factor that will influence the decision.

“Without news which softens the risks to inflationary pressures, I can see the argument for a further increase in rates and thereafter taking a more conditional approach,” he said, according to the MPC minutes.

However, he played down the likelihood of a prolonged series of increases, as markets have been predicting. “Today’s increase shouldn’t be seen as the first in an inevitable long sequence in hikes. But unless the conflict in the Middle East is resolved, neither does it seem likely to be the last increase,” he said.

The Bank’s next interest rate decision will be announced on 17 December, and some analysts suggested the MPC could press ahead with a pre-Christmas hike.

Andrew Goodwin, the chief economist at consultancy Oxford Economics , said: “The degree of inflationary pressure already in the system means another hike in December or February is likely.”

Explaining its decision to raise borrowing costs, the MPC highlighted the pass-through from elevated oil prices to business and consumer costs across the economy. It expects the Ofgem energy cap to rise from the equivalent of £1,723 a year for an average household in Great Britain to £2,150 in January and to increase again in April. Food price inflation could hit 4.75% by mid-2027, it warned.

Businesses have so far reported in the Bank’s surveys that they have been able to absorb soaring oil and gas prices – by hedging their energy costs, for example – but the MPC believes they will soon have to start passing them on to consumers in higher prices.

It is also concerned about workers seeking to offset the impact of the higher cost of living by asking for bumper pay rises.

after newsletter promotion

Oil prices have fallen sharply, to below $100 a barrel, after the Democrats’ victories in the US Congress, which some investors have interpreted as potentially constraining Donald Trump’s capacity to prolong the conflict in Iran. Trump’s vice-president, JD Vance, has blamed the war, and its impact on inflation, for the rout at the polls.

Speaking at the Bank’s press conference, Bailey welcomed the sharp fall in energy prices in the last 48 hours but said it would need to be sustained to change his view about the need for future rate rises. “This is positive news, but there is already a significant amount of inflationary pressure in the pipeline,” he said, adding: “What is the best thing that can happen? It is to resolve the conflict in the Middle East.”

While the decision to increase rates was supported by all MPC members, the minutes of the meeting reveal stark divisions over how much further they may need to go to bring inflation under control. The dovish Alan Taylor suggested this should be a “risk-management ‘one-for-now’ insurance hike”, while Mann argued that an immediate half-point rise was necessary to restore the Bank’s inflation-fighting credibility.

Healey’s budget included measures aimed at cushioning the impact of higher energy prices – including extending the fuel duty freeze and the VAT cut on electricity bills. The MPC said the package would shave a quarter percentage point off inflation in mid-2027.

Responding to the interest rate increase, Healey said: “The Iran conflict is reaching deep into the pockets of families and businesses here at home.

“In my budget I acted to give some breathing space to families and businesses. Twenty million households will get a £100 energy payment, I extended the tax cut on electricity bills and froze fuel duty. I also set out the course ahead to get costs down for good.”

But the shadow chancellor, Andrew Griffith, called the rate rise “another headwind for hardworking families to deal with”.

stories.body:
Foreign Office says 10-year sentence shows city’s security law is being used to ‘target individuals for political expression’

Hong Kong pro-democracy activist Joshua Wong sentenced to 10 years in prison in national security case

The UK and the US have condemned the 10-year sentence given to Hong Kong pro-democracy activist Joshua Wong under a controversial national security law.

Wong, 30, was sentenced on Thursday after pleading guilty to “foreign collusion” under the law. He is the only person to have been prosecuted twice under the legislation that critics say has been used to silence political opposition in the city.

A spokesperson for the UK Foreign Office said that Wong’s sentence was “a clear example of how the National Security Law is being used to target individuals for political expression and participation”.

The spokesperson added: “We call for an immediate end to all unjust prosecutions of individuals charged under the National Security Law and urge the authorities in China and Hong Kong to honour the rights and freedoms guaranteed to the people of Hong Kong under the Sino-British joint declaration (1984).”

The US consulate in Hong Kong said in a statement that it “strongly condemns” the additional sentence and called for Wong’s immediate release. “Wong has been unjustly imprisoned since December 2020, demonstrating that Beijing will go to extraordinary lengths to silence those who advocate for fundamental freedoms in Hong Kong,” a consular spokesperson said.

Shortly after the US consulate strongly condemned the sentence on Thursday, China warned “relevant parties” to “stop making irresponsible remarks” about Hong Kong judicial cases.

Human rights groups and politicians from across the political spectrum also criticised the sentence.

Elaine Pearson, Asia director at Human Rights Watch, said: “The harsh sentence on baseless charges against Joshua Wong is cruel and unjust. Young people promoting social change are an asset for any vibrant society, but the Hong Kong government puts them behind bars.”

Sarah Brooks, deputy regional director for Amnesty International, said: “Today’s sentence is another grim reminder of how Hong Kong’s National Security Law has become a tool to punish dissent rather than to genuinely protect national security.”

She said the new conviction “cruelly – and perhaps deliberately – comes mere months before he would have been eligible for release under his previous conviction”.

Wong has already spent six years in detention and had been due for release in January 2027.

In the most recent Foreign Office report on Hong Kong, published last month, the UK’s foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, said that Wong’s case “reinforced concerns about the increasingly broad application of national security legislation”.

Wong’s supporters called on governments around the world to push for his release.

Nathan Law , a Hong Kong activist and friend of Wong’s who was named as a co-conspirator in the case, said: “It’s incredibly sad to see my friend Joshua Wong suffer another sentencing over his peaceful advocacy work for Hong Kong’s democracy.”

Law called the sentencing “a farce” which signified that China “is determined to quash any hopes for freedom and democracy on its soil”.

When former British colony Hong Kong was handed to China in 1997, it was promised 50 years of “one country two systems”, under which the city would keep some autonomy and freedoms.

The UK considers Beijing to be in violation of that international treaty, after the crackdown on protests in 2019 and 2020, and the sweeping legal reforms that followed.

Conservative MP Iain Duncan Smith said Wong had “stood up” for that treaty, which he said China had “subsequently trashed”.

He added: “Despite this, the UK government has done little to nothing about it. The more we give in when China breaks the rules, the worse it gets in the future.”

The Labour MP James Naish said: “Hongkongers in my constituency chose Britain for the freedoms Joshua is jailed for defending – values we should all support. This is not a lenient sentence and the government must show China that Britain will not tolerate it.”
