stories.body:
Unaccompanied asylum-seeking children are under 18s who arrive in the Uk without a parent or guardian.

Published 6 November 2026

Highland Council says a Home Office algorithm has allocated it with a "significant increase" in unaccompanied asylum-seeking children to look after.

The local authority said it had received national recognition for its work with the young people, many of them fleeing war or persecution.

But it said the rise in numbers would be challenging due to a lack of housing in its area, adding that the algorithm did not take into account the local situation.

The Home Office said councils had a statutory duty to support children arriving in the UK without a parent or guardian, and it was committed to working closely with authorities to help them meet their obligations.

More stories from the Highlands and Islands

News from the Highlands and Islands on BBC Sounds

Unaccompanied asylum-seeking children (UASC) are those under the age of 18 who arrive in the UK to apply for international protection on their own, without the support of an adult.

Many of them are fleeing their homeland because of political or religious persecution, war or famine.

There are 380 UASCs being looked after in Scotland, according to Scottish government figures for 31 July 2025 , external .

Highland Council is currently responsible for 72.

The council said it was contacted by local authorities body Cosla in July about a revised Home Office rota allocation formula.

In a report , external , officials said this had presented it with "significant challenges" and five times its previous number of UASCs.

Previously, Highland Council took into its care system one child per cycle, but this has now gone up to five.

There can be a period of two weeks to a number of months between cycle, depending on how many children arrive in the UK.

'Not an adequate tool'

Highland Council officials added: "The Home Office algorithm by itself is not an adequate tool without some understanding of local conditions.

"For example, the fact that Highland has significant housing challenges, both in terms of housing availability and cost, coupled with a lack of available workforce, means Highland is not an attractive option for asylum support providers."

The local authority has previously said its area needs an extra 24,000 houses over the next 10 years . New homes are needed to address a long-standing shortage of affordable homes.

The officials also said the Home Office had not so far placed any adult asylum seekers in the Highlands.

"This lack of adult asylum seekers in Highland has had the effect of increasing the number of UASC in 2026," they said.

In June, the UK government scrapped plans to house up to 300 male asylum seekers at Cameron Barracks in Inverness .

'Shared fairly'

Eligible UASCs, like other young people in foster, kinship or residential care can remain under local authority care up to the age of 21.

Some care leavers are eligible for support up to their 26th birthday.

Highland Council receives core funding of £143 per child, per day for under 18s. For over 18s it is £270 per week.

The Home Office said it was a priority to ensure vulnerable children received the care and support they needed.

A spokesperson said: ''Local authorities have a statutory duty to support unaccompanied asylum-seeking children and care leavers, and we are committed to working closely with them to help them meet these obligations.

"Through the National Transfer Scheme, we work with local authorities across the UK to ensure responsibility for supporting unaccompanied children is shared fairly."

stories.body:
Polling done for the Guardian shows plummeting support from a former key constituency of Donald Trump’s base

Q&A: Ask your questions about Democrats’ win in the midterms

Polling conducted by the Harris Poll for the Guardian before the election shows just how angry voters were and points to one key reason Republicans lost so badly: plummeting support from rural voters, once a key constituency of Donald Trump’s base.

Over the summer, 95% of Americans indicated they believed there was an affordability crisis , particularly because of steep gas and grocery prices. By October, 61% of voters believed the country was experiencing a recession, even though technically it wasn’t.

It’s hard to ignore the impact inflation has had on this election. Key voters had expressed for months deep discontent with what had become the status quo. Loggers in Maine said that tariffs against Canada were hurting their already-battered industry. Drivers in Texas facing three-hour commutes to work were spending $400 a month on gas. Farmers across the midwest said diesel prices were exacerbating a growing season beleaguered by drought.

Recent data showed the flip wasn’t just seen among Democrats and independents, who have held pessimistic views on the economy since Trump returned to office, but among some Republicans, too.

In February, right before the war in Iran began, 49% of Republicans said the economy was getting better. By October, that number would drop to just 28%.

The pain seemed especially acute for rural voters, long considered a core base for Trump.

The president had gained many of his supporters by angling himself as a successful businessman who would be an outsider in Washington. But soaring gas and diesel prices have been a major pain point in parts of the country where driving long distances is an everyday part of life.

Rural voters were much more likely to say that gas prices were hurting their finances and that they were in economic “survival mode”, or that one surprise bill could sink them, compared with their urban and suburban counterparts. They were also slightly more likely to say that Republicans had a bigger problem with corruption, or elected officials using their position for personal financial gain, than Democrats.

In the month before the midterms, the number of rural Americans who said the economy was getting worse climbed 17% since Trump took office, compared with a 5% increase for those in the suburbs and a 3% jump among urban voters.

Yet on the eve of the midterm elections, Trump was trying to speak a different reality into existence, one where gas prices were going down, wages were rising and the US’s trade with other countries had never been stronger.

“I’ve traveled all across the country, spoken at all of these rallies I’ve done over the last two and a half weeks, and America is ready to go. They’re ready to vote,” Trump said in front of the Lincoln Memorial’s Reflecting Pool on Monday. “I hope they’re ready to do the right thing.”

But the reality that Americans have been facing is vastly different, and Americans responded accordingly. Republicans in key races from Maine to Texas lost their toss-up races on Tuesday, and Democrats will have control of Congress for the next two years.

Democrats have promised they will be busy trying to address the issues that were at the forefront of the election: the Trump administration’s brutal immigration crackdown, corruption in the White House, rising healthcare costs and the economy, specifically higher prices.

Republicans are just starting to take stock of the role prices had on the election outcome. JD Vance on Wednesday said the loss was the “cost to pay” for the Iran war. “Any honest conversation about where we go from here must start there,” Vance said.

As much as the midterms were a “blue-nami” for Democrats, pre-midterm polls showed voters were still unsure about the party’s ability to deal with affordability. When asked which party had the solution to the affordability crisis a month before the election, 34% said that neither party had a solution. Democrats (27%) slightly edged out Republicans (24%), but many voters seemed unsure whether any party could deal with these pocketbook issues.

Similar polling conducted before the 2024 presidential election showed that key independent voters were feeling just as pessimistic about the economy. Inflation had reached a generational high in 2022, and many Americans felt that Biden and Democrats weren’t doing enough.

Price increases under Trump, particularly after the Iran war, have only gotten worse. But many voters are dealing with years of economic burnout and will expect results in the coming years.

stories.body:
US tech stocks open higher after Thursday's rout

Ding ding goes the Wall Street opening bell, and trading is underway after the US stock market’s most bruising day in 19 months yesterday.

And it’s a mixed picture!

Tech stocks are rising, lifting the Nasdaq up by 1.2% in early trading. AI-linked stocks such as AMD (+8.1%), SanDisk (+8.3%) and Nvidia (+6.5%) are among the top risers.

But the much-storied Dow Jones Industrial Average (DJIA) is moving the other way, down 1% at the open. It’s being dragged down by old-economy stocks such as Nike (-3.5%), Walmart (-3.2%) and McDonalds (-3.1%).

Reminder: Yesterday the Nasdaq index slumped by 5.5%, while the DJIA dropped by 3.44%. So this is only a small recovery for the Nasdaq , and further pain for the Dow .

Nasdaq posts fourth weekly fall in a row

And finally…. the Nasdaq’s mini-recovery from its post-midterms plunge is complete.

The main US tech index has closed for the night up 1.09%, with a gain of 264 points to end at 24,579 points.

But the broader picture is that the Nasdaq Composite has now fallen for four weeks running, as some of the air has come out of the AI bubble…

We’ll find out on Monday whether the recovery continues, or the sell-off resumes…. Goodnight. GW

Tech stocks still higher in afternoon trading

A late update: With two hours to go before Wall Street closes, the tech rebound continues.

The Nasdaq Composite index, which sank into ‘correction territory’ yesterday, is up 1.3% now.

Aerospace manufacturer and launch service provider Rocket Lab are the top riser, up 12.5%, followed by Airbnb (+11.7%), AppLovin (+10%), Advanced Micro Devices (+9.3%) and Intel (+8.9%).

But…. Fawad Razaqzada, market analyst at Stonex Trading and FOREX.com, says AI concerns linger, explaining:

double quotation mark Technology stocks staged a sharp recovery on Friday after yesterday’s brutal sell-off wiped trillions of dollars off global equity valuations. All major AI-related stocks – Nvidia, AMD, Broadcom and Core Weave – bounced back. But whether recovery holds is another matter. After Thursday’s brutal sell-off wiped trillions of dollars off global equity valuations. Today’s bounce has carried the Nasdaq 100 straight back into former support, and the worries behind the rout, from AI regulation to the sheer scale of tech spending, have not gone away. With the index still carving out lower highs and lower lows, we maintain a cautious Nasdaq 100 forecast, and the near-term risk remains tilted to the downside.

Here’s a late take on this week’s sell-off, from Lee Robinson, CIO of Altana Downside Protector Fund and founder of Altana Wealth:

double quotation mark “This sell off has been a long-time coming, and it is not just caused by the midterms or an unwinding of positions in the tech giants. What we are seeing today is the result of stretched valuations and last month’s re-pricing in credit markets, specifically the rising Credit Default Swaps of the Magnificent Seven and CoreWeave. Credit is the engine of capital markets which equities will always eventually follow. We launched the Altana Downside Protector to trade a major downturn that we could see playing out over the next 18 months. The key questions now are who gets hurt by this selloff and what happens next. We see a lot of risk being held by life insurers who are some of the largest owners of AI-linked private credit funds and could be facing a series of de-ratings across their balance sheets.”

[Credit default swaps are an insurance contract that pays out if a company defaults on its debt, as covered in The Big Short ].

Closing post

With European stock markets closed after a nervy day, and Wall Street calmer than yesterday, it’s time to wrap up…

European stock markets fell sharply today as a rout in US tech stocks spread across the Atlantic, after the Democrats’ midterms victory sparked fears of a slowdown in the AI industry.

A sell-off on Wall Street on Thursday was followed by sharp falls in Asian stocks markets overnight. The investor sentiment then reached London, where the market was, at one stage, poised for its worst day since March.

The FTSE 100 index, which tracks blue-chip shares listed in London, was down as much as 254 points, or 2.35%, at 10,528 points during a wave of selling in morning trading. But by the close of the day it had recovered to a 1% fall, helped by a bounce in US stocks when Wall Street reopened.

Across Europe, there were similar losses: Germany’s Dax index has fallen by 2%, France’s Cac 40 has lost 0.8%, and Spain’s Ibex ended the day down 0.6%. Italy’s FTSE Mib fell 0.9%.

In Asia-Pacific markets, Japan’s Nikkei 225 index sunk 6% and South Korea’s Kospi index tumbled more than 6.5%.

“It’s actually a bit of a disaster,” said Christopher Forbes, the head of Asia and Middle East at CMC Markets.

double quotation mark “[Clients] were long index, long stocks, and they all got carried out. All night, all day – we had client margin calls, client complaints … because it’s a very emotional thing, right? People are wedded to their positions and views on a stock or outcome, and you’re telling them: ‘Look, you’ve just lost money.’”

Over in New York right now, the Nasdaq is up 1.5% (having fallen by 5.5% yesterday), and the S&P 500 is up 0.7%.

Here’s the full story:

Here’s the rest of today’s top business news:

Explainer: US tech stock rout: is the AI bubble bursting?

Global financial markets have been thrown into a tailspin as investors bet on an AI slowdown after the US midterm elections.

This is not the first time stock markets have wobbled in recent months due to concerns over a tech bubble. But could this volatility be the start of a huge market meltdown?

Read more here:

Europe’s other major stock markets also recovered some, but not all, of their earlier losses.

Germany’s Dax index has fallen by 2%, France’s Cac 40 has lost 0.8%, and Spain’s Ibex ended the day down 0.6%. Italy’s FTSE Mib fell 0.9%.

FTSE 100 closes down 1%

Phew! After a volatile day’s trading, the London stock market is closed.

And after an early slump, triggered by Thursday’s Wall Street rout, UK stocks have recovered some of their losses.

The FTSE 100 share index has closed for the night down 108.7 points, or 1%, at 10,673 points.

That will make a dent in millions of ISAs and pensions, but it’s not as bad as this morning’s worst point when the Footsie was down 2.35% and heading for its worst day since March.

The US dollar has strengthened further today, and is now up 0.65% against a basket of other currencies.

The London stock market has recovered some, but by not means all, of its earlier losses.

The FTSE 100 index is now down 145 points, or 1.35%, at 10,637 – having earlier been down as much as 2.35%.

Today’s better-than-expected US jobs report may be helping Wall Street to recover.

“This was a relatively strong jobs report across the board,” said Collin Martin , head of fixed income research and strategy at the Schwab Center for Financial Research.

double quotation mark “It may help calm some of the fears that spread to the markets yesterday on AI concerns, supporting the case that the economy remains strong.”

Elon Musk is clawing back some of the $113bn he’s lost in the previous two days ( see earlier post ).

Tesla’s shares are up 4.9%, while SpaceX have gained 6%, after both stocks fell by over 10% over Wednesday and Thursday.

Hargreaves Lansdown: our clients are buying the dip

Trading platform Hargreaves Lansdown reports that its clients have been “buying the dip” – the practice where investors pile in when a stock falls to tempting levels.

Anna Macdonald, investment strategy director at Hargreaves Lansdown, suggests this week’s tech selloff (which is already unwinding) is a buying opportunity:

Macdonald says:

double quotation mark “Trading interest in overseas AI and technology companies has been growing all week. We’ve seen some larger investors taking risk off the table, but the average trade has been a buy with Nvidia, SpaceX, Micron, AMD and Alphabet making up the top five. Nvidia and SpaceX are the headline names, while Micron and AMD give investors exposure to the hardware side of the story. Alphabet is interesting too, as its shares were marked down after disappointing numbers and clients have used that as an opportunity to buy. Overall, many of our clients are taking a long-term view and see this as a moment to get back into some of these names at a cheaper entry point. Yesterday’s sell-off looks like an overreaction. We’ve seen these wobbles before and we’ll see them again, but investors need to focus on the fundamentals. Demand for AI isn’t going away, and we expect the newly elected US officials to take a pragmatic approach to the buildout. For patient investors, this is an opportunity to invest in high-quality companies at valuations we haven’t seen in a long time.”

[We don’t do investment advice here at the Guardian, beyond Caveat emptor, dear readers.]

After a slow start, the S&P 500 index of US stocks is rising, up 1% today.

Wong, 30, in prison since 2020, is only activist in Hong Kong prosecuted twice under national security law

Exclusive: Joshua Wong laments city’s fate from inside maximum security prison

The Hong Kong activist Joshua Wong has been sentenced to 10 years in prison after earlier pleading guilty to “foreign collusion”, his second conviction under a national security law critics say has been used to silence political opposition in the city.

Wong, who rose to prominence as the teenage face of Hong Kong’s 2014 pro-democracy demonstrations, submitted his guilty plea in September. He had been accused of working with the exiled Hong Kong activist Nathan Law to urge foreign powers to impose sanctions, blockades or other hostile measures against China.

In his ruling on Thursday, the high ​court judge William Tam ‌described Wong’s actions as “grave in nature”.

He said Wong had visited the US to seek foreign interference before the national security law’s introduction in 2020, and continued to share posts on social media by Law calling for sanctions after it was enacted.

Wong’s role was to “supply his underground support” and “arouse the attention of foreign countries to bolster the cause”, the judge said. He described Wong’s actions as part of a “scheme” to collude with foreign governments.

Tam said Wong’s sentence would run concurrently with the remaining term of his previous national security offence.

After the ruling, Law said in a statement: “It’s incredibly sad to see my friend Joshua Wong suffer another sentencing over his peaceful advocacy work for Hong Kong’s democracy. The signal the sentencing sent to the world is that [China] is determined to quash any hopes for freedom and democracy on its soil.”

Amnesty International’s deputy regional director, Sarah Brooks, said: “Today’s sentence is another grim reminder of how Hong Kong’s national security law has become a tool to punish dissent rather than to genuinely protect national security.”

Wong wore a dark blue shirt and thick rimmed spectacles in court, and nodded and bowed as supporters waved. Dozens of people had waited in line outside the court building for the hearing, amid a heavy police presence. A group of international diplomats was also present for the sentencing.

The former student leader is already serving a prison term of four years and eight months, imposed in November 2024, for conspiracy to commit subversion for his role in an unofficial primary election. He has spent nearly six years in detention and had been due to be released in January 2027.

The US consulate in Hong Kong said in a statement that it “strongly condemns” the additional sentence and called for Wong’s immediate release. “Wong has been unjustly imprisoned since December 2020, demonstrating that Beijing will go to extraordinary lengths to silence those who advocate for fundamental freedoms in Hong Kong,” a consular spokesperson said.

Shortly afterwards, China warned against “irresponsible” remarks on Hong Kong’s judicial affairs. “Relevant parties should earnestly respect China’s sovereignty, respect Hong Kong’s legal system, stop making irresponsible remarks regarding the trial of … judicial cases,” the foreign ministry spokesperson, Guo Jiakun, told reporters.

Wong, 30, gained international attention during the 2014 Umbrella protests , which paralysed the city’s financial centre and galvanised a generation of young people. In October 2014, he appeared on the cover of Time magazine under the headline: “The face of protest.”

When protests erupted in 2019 over a proposed extradition bill, Wong was serving a prison sentence for his role in the 2014 demonstrations. He was released at the height of the protests and immediately took to the streets.

The following year, Beijing introduced a sweeping national security law it said was needed to restore stability to the former British colony, but critics say has been used to target political opposition, dissolve civil society groups and silence independent media.

Wong is the only activist in Hong Kong prosecuted twice under the law.

Bank’s decision goes contrary to analysis from Office for Budget Responsibility that predicts lower inflation and little impetus for wage growth

Bank of England raises interest rates to 4%

Business live – latest updates

An interest rate rise by the Bank of England to 4% is a big call when households are suffering from a second cost of living crisis in four years.

Many people will be incredulous when they hear of the decision to increase the cost of borrowing by 0.25 percentage points, looking around their neighbourhood for signs of a booming economy.

The official figures show the economy has proved resilient in response to the jump in oil and gas prices after the outbreak of war in Iran, but UK high streets are struggling and the underlying drivers of inflation are absent.

Most households are spending to stand still, whether it is on food, energy, holidays or leisure pursuits. Businesses are in much the same position. Like households, they have absorbed significant tax rises.

What the Bank’s policymakers believe is that despite all this, the energy price shock, being larger than first estimated, will surge through all parts of the economy, forcing up prices, encouraging a wave of wage demands that will, in turn, give inflation a second burst of life next year and the following year.

This analysis stands in contrast to the Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR), which acts as the Treasury’s independent forecaster. The OBR was clear in evidence to parliament on Wednesday that there was little impetus for strong wages growth.

The OBR said that, rather than economic growth next year of 1.6% and a rise in inflation to 4.9%, as the Bank expects, it believes the economy will expand by just 1% in 2027 and that the consumer prices index (CPI) will peak at just 3.75%. Inflation hit 3.5% in September, official figures showed .

The OBR’s chief economist, David Miles, said one of the main reasons for this assessment was the state of UK businesses, which he judged to be quite weak.

He said they had absorbed a large slice of the rise in energy and fuel costs, and their profit margins had plummeted on average as a result. Where once margins averaged 13% to 14%, the latest figures show they have fallen to 10% to 11%.

He said there would be little appetite to pay high wage settlements and the imperative would be to rebuild margins.

The wider economic situation is also very different from the previous crisis in 2022, when the country was coming out of the pandemic and dealing with the onset of the Ukraine war.

Back then, households were awash with lockdown savings that they wanted to spend, and firms were struggling to hire enough staff, leading to intense competition for workers and a spike in wages.

Today, savings are low and households bear the scars of four years of high inflation.

What sectors of the economy are making hay in 2026? Retailers and hospitality businesses are suffering, transport companies are battered by high costs and the charity sector is facing widespread financial difficulties. Vacancies are low, suggesting that firms have no need to employ more people.

Businesses in better-performing sectors such as banking and oil and gas also show little appetite for big wage increases. Banks are using artificial intelligence to shed staff .

The deputy director of the British Chambers of Commerce, David Bharier, said he was dismayed by the decision.

“So far, there is little sign of the wage-price spiral the Bank is looking to guard against. Unemployment is higher than in 2022, the labour market is looser and our research shows AI adoption accelerating rapidly – with some of the deepest users more likely to expect headcount reductions,” he said.

“After a budget which gave businesses little incentive to invest, and with borrowing costs already high, it is economic growth that will pay the premium.”

The Bank’s own survey of businesses and a separate report from its regional agents indicate “that wage and price expectations have moved little since September”.

It means Threadneedle Street policymakers judge that responses to their own business review will prove inaccurate and wages will jump.

The Bank judged that households’ and firms’ “attentiveness” to rising inflation was high and “there was a risk wage settlements would be higher than businesses expect”.

When the government says it is constrained by the bond markets from spending more to help consumers, there is a scenario looming in which ministers and the central bank, to meet their individual mandates, effectively crush the prospects for economic growth.

John Healey will say, as he did at the dispatch box last week, that he needs to restrict borrowing and adhere to his fiscal rules. Meanwhile, the bank will be busy making sure it cracks down on inflationary pressures it believes are on the way, even if policymakers cannot see them quite yet.

stories.body:
Essex county councillor Carl Johnson wrote on Facebook that "no foreigner should ever be allowed to stand for political office in this country"

Published 6 November 2026

A Reform UK councillor has been labelled a "racist" and accused of posting "xenophobic conspiracy theories" by a Labour councillor, after questioning whether migrants and their children should be allowed to stand for elected office.

Essex county councillor Carl Johnson posted a picture of Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood next to London Mayor Sadiq Khan, and wrote "we have been deliberately infiltrated".

Labour county councillor Lee Scordis called on Reform to "expel him immediately".

Johnson and his party have both since defended his right to free speech.

"Open debate and free speech should not be shut down simply because others disagree with a particular viewpoint," said Johnson, speaking to the Local Democracy Reporting Service (LDRS).

Johnson shared the image of the two prominent Labour politicians on Wednesday.

In his accompanying message, he wrote: "We have allowed people who arrived as asylum seekers to settle and then have second generations, gain positions of political power, and then push to change our laws to better reflect their own religion and culture.

"That is unacceptable. No foreigner should ever be allowed to stand for political office in this country."

The Facebook post has since been removed from the page of councillor Carl Johnson and the BBC contacted him for a response.

'Personal views'

Both the home secretary and London mayor were born in the UK and are the second generation of migrant families.

Scordis said the Reform councillor had suggested that politicians like Winston Churchill and Rishi Sunak, who had at least one parent born abroad, "could not be elected in any role, let alone prime minister".

A Reform spokesperson said: "[The party] is committed to net-negative migration and will prioritise the needs of the British people.

"Councillor Johnson is entitled to his own personal views."

The Reform councillor's post included a picture of Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood, next to London Mayor Sadiq Khan (these are not the images he shared)

The Braintree Conservatives said they "strongly oppose these remarks, and the obsession of some Reform politicians openly challenging the identity of Britons born in this country".

Meanwhile, Essex County Council said it was "aware of the social media post by councillor Carl Johnson" but would not comment on whether a complaint had been received.

Johnson told the LDRS: "My concern is that individuals who hold positions of political influence in the UK should always act in the interests of this country and its people.

"There have been well-publicised cases where questions have been raised about political figures advocating positions that appear to place the interests of other countries, cultures or ideologies above those of the United Kingdom."

Six moves Reform has made since taking power in Essex Published 6 June

The home secretary's parents immigrated from Kashmir, and Khan's from Pakistan.

Earlier this year, Mahmood told the BBC that friends and family had recently experienced racist slurs "when they had gone 20 years without hearing those words said to them".

"I think we're living in a more divisive, more polarised world. I think social media has a lot to do with sending hateful, divisive stuff through the algorithms," she said, speaking in January.

Johnson did not refer to them directly in his post, but the image he shared of them included the caption: "One changing our capital city, the other bringing in Islam in the thousands."

The Facebook post, before it was removed, had received 14,000 interactions and more than 3,000 comments.

He is the county councillor for Three Fields and Great Notley, which includes MDP Wethersfield, where hundreds of asylum seekers are accommodated.

The Reform leader of Essex County Council Peter Harris has also been approached for comment.

stories.body:
Exclusive: pro-democracy activist’s prison letters reveal fascination with AI, brushes with Triads and an appetite for books

Hong Kong pro-democracy activist Joshua Wong sentenced to 10 years in prison in national security case

F rom inside Hong Kong’s oldest maximum security prison, where he swaps books with Triad gang members and studies law, Joshua Wong writes letters like a man desperate to stay connected to the outside world.

Excerpts from his private prison writings reveal the pro-democracy activist asking friends to take screenshots of social media accounts and put questions to AI chatbots on his behalf.

To one acquaintance, he writes about his prison reading habits. “Some of the old-school triad bosses in here have also lent me books,” he says in the letters to friends, seen exclusively by the Guardian. “They read too. One of them lent me Mario Puzo’s The Godfather (lol).”

The 30-year-old Wong, who rose to prominence as the teenage face of Hong Kong’s now-squashed democracy movement, has been imprisoned since November 2020.

On Thursday, he was sentenced to 10 years for foreign collusion , his second conviction under the national security law imposed by Beijing in 2020. Wong pleaded guilty to the charge in September.

Wong is the only pro-democracy activist to be prosecuted twice under the national security legislation. He had been due to be released in January, before the latest prosecution, and will now serve his two sentences concurrently.

Despite spending his 21st, 25th and 30th birthdays in prison, Wong’s letters – written between August and October – show his resolve and continuing concern about Hong Kong’s future.

“The only thing I worry about is that people will forget Hong Kong, and that amid competition and struggles between great powers, they will forget the countless ordinary, unknown people in different places who have paid a price for their beliefs,” he writes.

In Stanley prison, where young inmates use M&Ms as currency, he spends time exercising, learning to play the guitar and teaching English to other prisoners.

“I was teaching English to a Russian,” he says in one letter. “When he asked me what the word ‘totalitarian’ meant, I simply answered, ‘Putin’ (lol)”.

Books appear to be central to his life. His reading list includes Patriot, the memoir of Russian opposition leader, Alexei Navalny, who died in prison in 2024; biographies of Steve Jobs, Nelson Mandela, Benjamin Franklin; and the memoir of former Citibank trader turned YouTuber and inequality campaigner, Gary Stevenson.

On the day of the US presidential election in November 2024, he watched votes come in while holding a copy of JD Vance’s bestselling memoir, Hillbilly Elegy.

Wong gained international attention during the 2014 Umbrella protests , which paralysed the city’s financial centre and galvanised a generation of young people. In October 2014, he appeared – with his trademark black-rimmed spectacles – on the cover of a Time magazine under the headline: “The Face of Protest”.

When protests erupted in 2019 over a proposed extradition bill, Wong was serving a prison sentence for his role in the 2014 demonstrations. He was released at the height of the protests and immediately took to the streets.

In 2020, Beijing said its introduction of the national security law was needed to restore stability to the former British colony, but critics said it gave authorities sweeping powers to crack down on free speech and dissent.

Since then, activists and journalists have been arrested, independent newsrooms closed, and much of the city’s political opposition forced into exile . There have been more than 400 arrests under national security legislation, according to Hong Kong’s security bureau.

“Joshua’s case is part of an attempt to control how my generation’s political history is remembered,” says Frances Hui, a childhood friend and pro-democracy activist in exile.

“For years, people around the world could hear him argue, organise, and explain what he thought Hong Kong’s future should be. Now we can barely hear from him at all.”

In his letters, Wong says Mandela inspired him to study law and he has enrolled in an undergraduate company law course.

He says that he has lost weight, but has a strict routine of pull-ups, squats and pushups. He also reads the Bible and recites passages from the book of Joshua and the Corinthians.

Wong’s childhood friends and fellow activists say the Hong Kong they once fought for no longer exists.

“It is hard to say whose side time is on,” says another childhood friend, who spoke on condition of anonymity for fear of reprisal.

Hui says that Hong Kong authorities had waited nearly five years after the alleged crime to prosecute Wong – just before his release.

“By the time he sees freedom, he is most certainly not going to be the young boy we once remembered,” she says.

stories.title: Thatcher's Right to Buy created a generation of homeowners - did it also fuel the housing crisis?
stories.summary: Labour is weakening Margaret Thatcher's landmark housing policy. Will it really fix Britain's social housing woes?
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Thatcher's Right to Buy created a generation of homeowners - did it also fuel the housing crisis?

Published 6 November 2026

Growing up in a council flat in the 1980s and 1990s, my mum would often point out homes that tenants had bought from the council. You could usually tell just from looking. A plain wooden door had been replaced with something fancier. New windows had appeared. Sometimes there was a porch or pillars outside the front door.

Those houses were bought under the Right to Buy scheme - arguably the most consequential housing policy of my lifetime. It was introduced in 1980, three years before I was born, when Margaret Thatcher's government gave council tenants in England the legal right to purchase their homes at a discounted price.

Supporters welcomed the chance for working-class families to own their own home and build wealth. Critics argue it hollowed out the country's stock of social housing and contributed to today's housing crisis.

Some of my neighbours "made a killing" from the policy, in the words of my mum. One bought an almost identical flat to ours in 1989 for £21,200, after receiving a discount of £18,800. Eight years later it sold for £54,500. Five years after that it changed hands again for £143,000. (Notably, the person who made the most money from that flat wasn't the original council tenant - it was the people who bought it afterwards.)

The writer grew up in a council flat in north London - and recently returned there, 25 years later

But Andy Burnham doesn't like the policy. The Right to Buy scheme has seen various changes since its introduction in the 1980s, and Labour has weakened it significantly since coming to power in 2024. Then, in September, the prime minister told Labour's conference: "We will reform Right to Buy. Not taking the right away from anyone in an existing home, but removing it from new homes." This would help to keep council houses in public ownership "for generations to come", Burnham told delegates.

He has previously compared trying to solve the housing crisis while continuing to sell social homes to "trying to fill a bath with the plug out".

More than 40 years after its introduction, Right to Buy remains a debate about political values as much as housing policy, balancing the home ownership ideal against the desire to preserve social housing for future generations.

A 'property-owning democracy'

Since 1980, more than two million homes have been sold through the scheme in England.

In fact, about 40% of England's council housing stock has been sold through Right to Buy. Most of those sales took place in the early years, says Prof Rebecca Tunstall, a housing academic at the University of York and London School of Economics. At the time, Labour was vehemently opposed to Thatcher's plans. Yet many of its own voters went on to benefit from them.

Labour now argues that not enough of those two million homes were replaced. Sir Keir Starmer's government restricted the scheme, including by heavily reducing the maximum discount that councils were allowed to give tenants.

And now Burnham is removing the right to buy entirely from any new-build social home. The measures are included in a bill currently making its way through Parliament. The government says that before Labour's various restrictions on the scheme, England was projected to see a net loss of 26,000 council homes over the next decade. Now there will be a net gain of 18,000 homes over the same period, it calculates.

This opens up a political divide: some opposition parties, like the Conservatives and Reform UK, say they would keep or even extend the scheme.

For those who became homeowners, Right to Buy turned a dream into reality.

Barbara Stevens, now 80, bought her two-bedroom council flat in Kentish Town, north London, through Right to Buy for around £35,000. Now mortgage-free, she estimates it could be worth between £600,000 and £700,000.

Margaret Thatcher launched Right to Buy a year after becoming prime minister, and spoke of her vision of a "property-owning democracy"

"I've always wanted to own my own property," she says.

Her friend Trevor Abrahmsohn believes her story demonstrates the success of the scheme. "If you want to condemn the poor to poverty, make them lifetime renters," he says.

Those arguments were central to Thatcher's vision of a "property-owning democracy".

Few people are more closely associated with Right to Buy than Lord Heseltine, who was the cabinet minister responsible for housing when it was introduced. When he and Thatcher launched the scheme in 1980, council tenants were offered substantial discounts to purchase their homes.

A relative of mine whose parents bought their council home in Croydon told me it was the only time "anyone would ever give you a hundred grand for free".

Even Housing Secretary Angela Rayner - part of the government that's restricting Right to Buy - bought and later sold her own council home for a profit.

In 1980, Lord Heseltine described the scheme as the biggest transfer of capital wealth from the state to ordinary people. "It certainly was," he says now, almost half a century on.

I ask him if, looking back, he would have designed the policy differently. "No," he answers.

He thinks Right to Buy gave its beneficiaries an important asset. "People who bought their own homes made a great deal of capital gain," he says.

A 'double charge' for taxpayers?

But to its detractors, Right to Buy is responsible for many of Britain's housing woes.

Prof Tunstall says the policy is partly responsible for making social housing scarcer, which meant more people competed for homes in the private rented sector, pushing up rents.

Lord Heseltine says it was originally assumed that councils would use sale proceeds to support new housing. He acknowledges that did not happen after he left government.

That failure to replace sold homes sits at the heart of the modern criticism of Right to Buy.

For Molly Harris from the New Economics Foundation, it is "private landlords [who] are the real winners".

Her think tank's research found that 41% of homes sold through Right to Buy are now privately rented out. "Homes that were built with public money, and with the aim of providing an affordable and secure path to home ownership, have since been turned into assets," Harris says.

Along with her brother (left) and other siblings, the writer says she enjoyed security in her family's rented council flat (right)

She says the shortage of social housing means more people need help with housing costs in the private rented sector, where rents are higher. So taxpayers are effectively paying twice: once to give a discount on the initial home; and then again, via housing benefit, when that home is rented out to someone who can't afford the payments. A former council home rented privately could now be valued at double, triple or quadruple what it cost when it was under local authority control.

I put that criticism to Lord Heseltine, asking him whether the scheme has failed because some ex-council homes are now effectively being rented back to the state, at higher costs.

He dismisses it as "rubbish", adding: "The scheme was wildly successful in spreading ownership across the country."

According to Harris's research, the government spent more than £58bn between 2021 and 2025 "subsidising private landlords" through the benefit system.

Newham Council says almost half of the 9,000 council homes sold under Right to Buy in Newham were later "flipped" into private rentals. The borough now has the biggest council house waiting list in the country. Last year, The Big Issue reported that Newham Council made a loss of more than £20m of taxpayers' money buying back homes it had sold just a few years earlier. The council said it was a quick way to provide new housing, and was a cheaper option than some alternatives.

And some council tenants say they are not interested in buying their homes. Ruth Crabb has lived in her flat in Havering since 1997. "I wouldn't buy my flat because I didn't want it to go out of circulation, as social housing is for those who come after me," she says. But, she adds: "I don't judge anyone who bought their property with Right to Buy."

The ownership premium

Supporters of Right to Buy also argue that you can't appreciate the true value of the scheme by looking at numbers on a spreadsheet.

The benefits of the policy extended for generations, they say, helping the children and grandchildren of those who bought homes.

Research co-authored by Matteo Sandi, an economics professor at the University of Milan, looked at children growing up in areas where Right to Buy uptake was highest. He found better educational and economic outcomes, including higher GCSE attainment, greater chances of attending university, and increased earnings in adulthood.

"What we find is that there is, in fact, a lasting benefit from growing up in an owned property," he says.

He believes it's because ownership encouraged families to invest more heavily in their homes and neighbourhoods.

One of my relatives backs this up. He tells me his parents were able to move elsewhere in the country, enjoy a better standard of living and finally afford things that had previously been out of reach. He believes Right to Buy transformed their lives.

Lord Heseltine, pictured here on a visit to Liverpool in 1981, says Right to Buy "spread ownership across the country"

But Prof Tunstall argues home ownership is not the only route to a stable family life. "The critical things for safety and for children's development and for happy families are security and affordability," she says - and children can also get that from social renting, she thinks.

Looking back, that resonates.

When I was a child and my mum rented from the council, she knew what she would be charged every month. She knew we wouldn't suddenly be forced to move. My siblings and I knew we wouldn't have to change schools. At that point, in the 1980s, one third of houses in England were council-owned. When my mum became pregnant with me, it was safe to assume that a home would soon become available - and within about a year, one did. She moved out of my nan's and into her new council flat.

The children I now meet through my work often do not have that certainty. Today, the average wait for a family-sized home in London is 27 years. Some children are moved repeatedly between hotels and hostels. Councils across England now spend £8m every day housing families in temporary accommodation.

Sandi is careful not to present his findings as an unconditional endorsement of Right to Buy.

"My take is the Right to Buy scheme was a good policy with a big limitation," he says. "More social housing should have been built."

Lots of former council estates have been partly privatised as a result of Right to Buy

But curbing Right to Buy could take a long time to bear fruit, says Prof Tunstall. Scotland abolished its Right to Buy programme in 2016 and Wales followed in 2019 - but Prof Tunstall says it "hasn't made a huge difference" yet in those nations, because the changes are too recent. (Northern Ireland continues to operate a scheme similar to Right to Buy.)

And deeper challenges will remain; Right to Buy is not the only culprit of Britain's social housing shortage, she says. Supply has also been reduced by council estate-clearance programmes, she says, which saw thousands of homes demolished from the 1990s. Like Lord Heseltine, she also blames decades of under-building: had governments continued to build at their 1980s rates, she argues, the sale of council homes might not have resulted in an overall loss of social housing.

The housing landscape has also changed dramatically since 1980. Many councils transferred responsibility over council housing to housing associations, meaning they have lost the skills and expertise to build their own stock.

More than 25 years later, I return to the street where I grew up. It looks much the same, although a few new front doors suggest more homes have been sold. My mum never took advantage of Right to Buy; she continues to rent a council flat on a small estate in south London.

I ask her if she regrets that. She says she simply wouldn't have been able to afford it.

HS2 blew billions - here's how and why Published 2 days ago

Young adults are taking prescription drugs instead of alcohol - and it's dividing experts Published 18 August

Publicly owned rail is popular. But is it making the trains run on time? Published 13 October

I tell her that the flat she could have bought for around £20,000 would now be worth somewhere between £350,000 and £400,000.

"You're kidding?," she replies.

No-one in the 1980s could have known what would happen to house prices or the cost of living.

But whatever people think about Right to Buy, there is broad agreement on one point: the problem was not necessarily selling the homes. It was failing to replace them.

stories.title: The Bantu expansion changed Africa. Scientists are still tracing how.
stories.summary: Genes and archaeology are revealing how Bantu speakers spread across much of Africa.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Genes and archaeology are revealing how Bantu speakers spread across much of Africa.

It’s not easy to extract iron from its ore. But the peoples of the ancient city of Great Zimbabwe—the capital of a thriving kingdom in southern Africa between 1000 to 1700 AD—were masters.

At sites near the city’s stone ruins, clusters of iron-smelting furnaces survive today as mounds of rubble. At Mashava, a village 25 miles northwest, fragments bear fingermarks of those who long ago smoothed the structures’ clay interiors.

Some of the furnaces were nearly an adult’s arm span in width, with walls thick and strong to contain the heat of more than 2,100° Fahrenheit needed to smelt iron. Unlike other furnaces that required workers to force air into them with bellows, these were designed to suck air in, then out through a chimney, no human labor required. This would have made it significantly easier to produce the iron, which was fashioned into hoes, axes, and arrowheads.

“The number and size of these furnaces, together with the use of natural-draft technology, indicate intensive and technologically sophisticated iron production,” says archaeometallurgist Ezekiel Mtetwa of Chicago’s Field Museum of Natural History, who has long studied the furnaces .

Scientists are extremely interested in the peoples who created this and other iron-powered societies across eastern and southern Africa. Research points to an adaptable and innovative group from western Africa as the masterminds. Known as Bantu speakers, these communities began gradually expanding across the continent’s southern half, starting from 6,000 to 4,000 years ago. In doing so, they introduced a fundamentally new, sedentary way of life—characterized by farming, raising livestock, pottery-making, and metalworking—to regions previously dominated by hunter-gatherer communities.

This migration transformed not only the region’s history and technology, but also its languages: Today, around 350 million Africans speak one of roughly 500 distinct Bantu tongues, from southern African Zulu to eastern African Swahili. And at least as many Africans—as well as many African Americans and Afro-Latinos—carry Bantu ancestry in their DNA.

Reconstructing this expansion has been a tough puzzle, especially given the region’s sparse written historical records and limited research funding . But a unique blend of scientists—linguists, archaeologists, and geneticists—have teamed up to unearth clues about the deep origins of the Bantu-speaking people, their path across Africa, and their relationships with other cultures. Although much debate and uncertainty remain, little by little the work is uncovering one of history’s largest and longest human migrations.

“It completely reshaped the demography in sub-Saharan Africa, and we are really interested in trying to understand it,” says population geneticist Sandra Beleza of the United Kingdom’s University of Leicester.

People on the move

The first evidence of the Bantu expansion came from observations of similarities among Bantu languages. They’re so alike, in fact, that when the Portuguese explorer Vasco da Gama sailed around the southern tip of Africa in 1497, a Portuguese crew member who had spent time in west-central Africa could reportedly communicate with locals in southeastern Africa.

Linguists working in the 19th century started referring to the language family as Bantu , the plural of muntu , meaning “human being” in many Bantu tongues. Later linguists reasoned that the languages stemmed from an ancestral people who migrated across the continent from western Africa, which harbors the greatest diversity of Bantu languages (as would be expected for where the languages originated).

Soon, archaeologists found supporting evidence: across eastern and southern Africa, pieces of pottery of similar yet diverse styles, alongside first-time traces of village life, metal-making, domesticated animals, and western African crops—all developed within the last 2,000 years. Northern sites usually dated back to earlier time periods than sites farther south. “You can clearly see a north-to-south progression,” says archaeological scientist Shadreck Chirikure of the University of Oxford.

By the 1990s, however, some scholars began to question the idea that Bantu languages and skills spread through a migration. Couldn’t these cultural habits have spread while people stayed in the same place, with hunter gatherer communities passing along new technologies, languages, and habits to each other?

Genetic techniques that could analyze people’s ancestry helped to resolve that debate. All of us share DNA with our relatives: 50 percent on average with siblings, 12.5 percent with cousins, 3.3 percent with second cousins, and so on. Though these proportions become minute the further back in time a shared common ancestor lived, statistical techniques can tease out patterns.

Sure enough, a 2009 genetic analysis of 2,432 Africans found that Bantu-speaking people from western, central, and southern Africa are much more closely related than one might expect given their geographic distance. And in 2024, a team of scientists analyzed the genomes of 1,763 Africans and found the greatest genetic diversity among Bantu speakers in western Africa. As distance from the region increased, diversity declined. “This is a typical signature of a population expanding from one place to another,” explains coauthor Carina Schlebusch, a geneticist at Uppsala University in Sweden.

Mysterious roots

But while linguistic and genetic data point to western Africa—particularly the Grassfields region of Cameroon—as the Bantu homeland, conclusive archaeological proof is thin. At the best-studied archaeological site in the Grassfields, a rock shelter called Shum Laka, pottery fragments appear dating from 7,000 to 6,000 years ago and become abundant by 5,000 to 4,000 years ago. Bowls and jars at first decorated simply with incisions and stamps and later bearing the marks of carved or braided tools rolled over wet clay are a possible, yet inconclusive , trace of Bantu ancestors.

South of Cameroon, archaeologists have searched for artifacts in one of the Bantu-speaking people’s first destinations: the Congo rainforest. A handful of times between 2010 and 2023, archaeologist Alexandre Livingstone Smith of Belgium’s Royal Museum for Central Africa traveled via boat along the Congo River as part of a team led by linguist Birgit Ricquier. In a number of villages, Smith found pottery shards of a style consistent with that found farther west, dating back to 2,300 to 2,000 years ago. “That would be the potential first Bantu settlers of the forest,” Smith says.

Many experts interpret the trails of pottery as evidence that ceramics traditions were brought by Bantu-speaking people all the way from their original home. What’s unclear, however, is when and how Bantu-speaking peoples acquired their farming and metalworking skills—and, in particular, whether they invented iron smelting themselves or learned it from neighboring, iron-extracting cultures .

Scientists have been able to deduce the path that Bantu speakers took to eastern and southern Africa. Some scholars have argued that the path split into two before entering the Congo rainforest, with one group heading east while another went south through the forest. But evidence is now mounting that these groups crossed the rainforest together, and only upon reaching its southern fringes roughly 2,500 to 3,500 years ago did they split into east-moving and southward-moving groups.

Some of this evidence comes from linguistic studies. Not unlike the evolution of species, languages diverge and transform over time, creating “trees” that linguists can reconstruct from similarities in grammar and vocabulary. In 2015, a group of researchers did this computationally using data from about 400 Bantu languages . They observed a much larger diversity—and deeper splits—among the Bantu languages spoken in the Congo rainforest, suggesting that Bantu-speaking ancestors spent a long time there, allowing their languages to diversify. Languages spoken farther east and farther south appeared to stem from a less diverse subset of this larger group, explains coauthor Koen Bostoen, a linguist at Belgium’s Ghent University.

Later linguistic studies , as well as genetic analyses, have reached similar conclusions. In 2023, Beleza and her colleagues compared the genomes of Bantu speakers from Angola —south of the Congo rainforest—with those from the eastern African country of Mozambique and ones from Cameroon, the Bantu homeland.

Remarkably, the eastern African samples were more genetically similar to those from Angola, hundreds of miles to the south of Cameroon and south of the rainforest, than to any of the samples from Cameroon. That points to a recent common ancestor in the Angola region—suggesting that the Bantu split into eastern and southern streams only once they reached the rainforest’s southern edge, Beleza explains.

By the time the Bantu people commenced their movement east and south, they had already come into their own as a farming, iron-making, livestock-herding, and pottery-making people, Chirikure says: Many ancient Bantu settlements across eastern and southern Africa contain evidence of this Bantu “package.”

Mixing and mingling

Key to the Bantu’s success in southern and eastern Africa, experts suspect, was their sedentary lifestyle. This—and their iron tools—would have allowed them to produce more food and grow in number, propelling them to occupy new territories. Their lifestyle affected the landscape as forests turned into farmland , and it also affected the hunter-gatherer communities who were already living there. Some groups were likely crowded out and disappeared, experts suspect, while others were probably pushed to marginal regions, including Indigenous groups such as rainforest hunter-gatherers and Khoisan peoples, who continue to live in central and southern Africa, respectively, to this day.

Still, scientists are learning that Bantu peoples had deep relationships with these two groups. In the 2024 genetic analysis, Schlebusch and her colleagues found that some Bantu-speaking groups in central Africa share about an eighth of their DNA with rainforest hunter-gatherers, and some southern African Bantu speakers share a similar amount with Khoisan groups. Clearly, their ancestors once intermixed.

Curiously, in the case of the Khoisan, this mixing tended to arise from pairings of Bantu-speaking men with Khoisan women. One 2021 study of southern African Bantu speakers found that the DNA inside their mitochondria—which people inherit only from their mothers—had greater-than-expected proportions of Khoisan DNA. But the Y chromosomes, which come from fathers, had much higher proportions of DNA with Bantu ancestry. Some experts speculate that this pattern could be the result of Bantu men raiding Khoisan women or preferentially marrying Khoisan women for whom the traditional bride prices would have been cheaper. “Whenever there is a power difference… between two groups, it tends to melt down to this,” says coauthor Ananyo Choudhury, a geneticist at the University of Witwatersrand in South Africa.

This pattern also left marks on the language. The characteristic clicks of Khoisan languages also occur in southern African Bantu languages Zulu and Khosa. Bostoen suspects that the children of Khoisan-Bantu pairings were, at first, bilingual. Eventually, “they lost their mothers’ languages, but they left a substrate of the mothers’ languages in the Bantu language.”

Archaeologists are also studying the relationships between Bantu farmers and their neighbors. While there may have been conflicts over land, the groups also cooperated with and learned from one another, says Décio Muianga, an archaeologist at Eduardo Mondlane University and the research institute Kaleidoscopio in Maputo, Mozambique. He’s been excavating a rock shelter in Mozambique containing thousands of years’ worth of stone tools, wild animal bones, and wild plant remains—telltale signs of hunter-gatherers living at the site. But interestingly, Bantu-style pottery also appears. “My assumption is that the hunter-gatherers were getting these ceramics from the farmers,” Muianga says. “They were interacting, communicating, and exchanging resources.”

There is evidence, too, for cultural exchanges: European anthropologists have reported that some Bantu-speaking groups would solicit San hunter-gatherers to conduct traditional rainmaking ceremonies , for example.

Bantu social networks eventually extended well beyond Africa. By 1100 to 1600 AD, many of the complex state societies that Bantu speakers built developed trade networks across the Indian Ocean. Archaeological data shows they imported Chinese porcelain and glass beads ; in return, they exported gold, ivory, and iron. In fact, a 12th century Muslim cartographer once wrote that iron from parts of southern Africa—likely referring to Great Zimbabwe’s iron-producing hinterlands, Mtetwa suspects—was deemed to be of much higher quality than that from other places like India.

Mtetwa has found evidence that iron smelters near Great Zimbabwe would add bone fragments to the furnaces, perhaps as part of a smelting-blessing ritual, but one with scientific merit: This material contains calcium, which can accelerate the separation of iron from the rest of the ore. That may be a testament to the Great Zimbabweans’ iron-smelting skills: “Some materials introduced within ritual or medicinal practices may simultaneously have had technically beneficial effects on the smelt,” says Mtetwa.

A future full of research

Though they’ve made great progress in reconstructing the Bantu world, scientists are aware of, and trying to address, the limitations of their research so far.

Linguistic studies, for instance, have been a popular tool to reconstruct Bantu history, but Bostoen cautions that very few Bantu languages have been documented thoroughly enough to definitively trace linguistic trees back in time. Linguists may never get a complete dataset, because some old branches of the Bantu language family may have died out .

Another limitation of computational Bantu language-family reconstructions is that they’ve usually assumed that languages have evolved in isolation after different Bantu groups separated. But there may have been extensive cross-pollination among languages as different groups met and interacted.

In fact, when linguists factored in the possibility of contact among Bantu languages in a 2026 study, they couldn’t reconstruct the diversification patterns described by previous linguists, says coauthor Igor Yanovich of the University of Vienna, who wrote about the challenges of Bantu linguistic studies in the 2025 Annual Review of Linguistics . In his view, linguists should first focus on thoroughly documenting Bantu languages before attempting to use them to understand Bantu history.

In hopes of adding new insights, Schlebusch is working to obtain DNA from ancient human remains. By revealing the identity of people who were living in particular places at particular times, this could help to elucidate when and where different Bantu communities moved into, overlapped with, or repopulated areas. “What we see more and more in genetic data is that the movement was probably complex—that it was these ‘spread over spread’ events,” Schlebusch says.

Archaeologists, for their part, hope to fill in the vast gaps in the archaeological record of sub-Saharan Africa—by both conducting new excavations and re-examining existing artifact collections for fresh insights. But all this work requires funding for research and laboratories , especially from African governments, says Chirikure; he, like many of his colleagues, has largely relied on funding from Europe, which is limited. Without more funding, “you are not generating fresh ideas, you are not formulating new hypotheses and testing them using some of the cutting-edge science,” he says.

Scientists from all three disciplines are hopeful that they will eventually tell the complete story of how an innovative people spread and diversified across sub-Saharan Africa, mixing traditions with those of earlier peoples and of others who still live there, to create myriad cultures, each one a unique blend of food, philosophy, language, music, and traditions. “If you travel from West Africa today all the way to East Africa, you have a unique cultural diversity that is very hard to find in many other parts of the world,” Muianga says. Combined with the legacy of other groups, he says, “this is the result of the Bantu migration.”

stories.title: 'Not my job to set a budget,' says secretary of state
stories.summary: Sir Chris Bryant is understood to have asked parties to commit to raising an extra £200m in income.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Sir Chris said it is the "legal responsibility and duty" of the executive to set a budget

Published 5 November 2026

The Northern Ireland secretary has said that it is not his "job" to set a budget and that it is the responsibility of the Northern Ireland Executive.

This comes after no resolution was reached in negotiations between executive parties and Sir Chris Bryant.

He is understood to have presented a set of conditions, including revenue raising, to be attached to any potential deal on a Stormont budget.

Sir Chris said: "They really have to take me seriously when I say there is no more money."

Seven months into this financial year the Northern Ireland Executive has still not agreed a budget.

Speaking after a series of one-to-one meetings, the First Minister Michelle O'Neill said there was still "no white smoke".

Democratic Unionist Party leader (DUP) Gavin Robinson said he felt there was a level of optimism that was "not matched by the reality inside" the room during talks.

Northern Ireland Secretary Sir Chris Bryant (right) greets Finance Minister John O'Dowd at Hillsborough Castle

Speaking on BBC Newsline , Sir Chris said it is the "legal responsibility and duty" of the executive to set a budget.

He described talks ending without agreement as "a bit frustrating" but added that he's still "hopeful".

He said: "I just wanted to get a move on" and added: "Whatever the total envelope is you have to live within it".

Sir Chris also said he would only set a budget for Northern Ireland if the executive parties asked him to.

"They should be able to put together their budget but they have to decide what their priorities are."

The Sinn Féin delegation was made up of Michelle O'Neill, John O'Dowd, Mary Lou McDonald and Caoimhe Archibald

After talks with the secretary of state, the first minister said that while there may be things dividing the executive, her party would persist in trying to get a budget deal done that allows public sector pay awards to be made for this year.

O'Neill also said she was getting "impatient" with the government and that she would take no lectures from it about managing finances.

Democratic Unionist Party leader Gavin Robinson said the secretary of state is "not moving"

The DUP leader said: "As it stands today, the secretary of state is not moving, the practical, honest reality of that is that without additional resource, there will not be a balanced budget".

Robinson added that "there will be no legal ability to do what it is we think the executive needs to do, and what we want it to do" without a budget.

Bryant says executive should improve 'discipline'

Stormont ministers argue the UK's devolution funding formula no longer delivers enough for them to balance their books.

The government had offered them an additional £525m this year, but they said it still left significant gaps in managing their spending pressures, particularly delivery of pay awards for public sector workers.

It is not clear what the shape of a final budget agreement could look like, with some parties insisting there is still scope to "reprofile" some of the financial package.

Bryant's conditions are believed to include the executive committing to £200m in additional revenue raising in 2027/28 and 2028/29.

He has also asked that they should improve "discipline" around promises and delivery of pay parity to public sector workers in Northern Ireland.

Health Minister Robbie Butler, UUP leader Jon Burrows and Steve Aiken spoke to the media outside Hillsborough

Ulster Unionist leader Jon Burrows said he did not want to sound "defeatist" and would continue to engage with the government.

But he said there was a real prospect that it would be resolved in time to avert the potential of strike action by health care workers waiting on pay uplifts for this year.

Speaking before talks with the secretary of state, Alliance's Agriculture Minister Andrew Muir said it is now "make your mind up time" for the executive.

"This needs to be resolved not in weeks or months, but days. We need to come to a final conclusion and give certainty to people who deserve proper pay but also in terms of investment in public services we need to get this done," he added.

Speaking on BBC NI's The View programme, Social Democratic and Labour Party (SDLP) leader Claire Hanna said a budget is "an agreement to take responsibility and an agreement to prioritise".

Her party, which is the official opposition in the legislative assembly, is "very clear about the severe constraints," she said, but added: "the fact is by not having a budget in month eight of this financial year, everybody who's trying to operate in that budget is running at 95%".

Where are the budget negotiations at?

Talks between the government and the executive parties have been taking place for several months now , but earlier this week O'Dowd warned that a "crunch point" is approaching.

On Tuesday, the executive met again, with O'Dowd saying afterwards that he planned to present a series of options to his ministerial colleagues in the days ahead about a way forward.

He did not divulge what those may be, but the government has already said no to a request from the executive to allow a larger chunk of the money in the three-year offer to be spent this year, referred to as "front-loading".

What happens in the absence of a budget?

Without an agreed budget, departments face operating on emergency spending restricted to 95% of the prior year, with warnings that funds could run out by January.

The secretary of state has also warned that a cost-of-living £100 payment cannot be made to households in Northern Ireland until an executive budget is agreed .

That came after the government announced its first budget under Andy Burnham last week, with Northern Ireland getting an additional £270m for public services as a result, of which £131m can be used this year.

Sir Chris has said that he is exploring contingency measures to allow him to pass a budget bill at Westminster, in the event that a deal cannot be reached to do so at Stormont.

Delivering net zero also at risk, say MPs as they call for centralised policy and funding for mines and diversification

The UK is “dangerously” dependent on China for critical raw materials needed for the military, renewable energy infrastructure and AI, a parliamentary investigation has found.

MPs on the business select committee called for an urgent centralised policy and the creation of a “critical minerals finance facility” to help fund rare earth and other critical mineral mines, and deploy grants, equity and debt to accelerate a diversification programme.

“Critical minerals are the alpha of the new economy,” said the committee’s chair, Liam Byrne. “We cannot rearm Britain, build AI or deliver net zero unless we secure the minerals these technologies depend on.

“Yet 16 years after China first weaponised its chokehold over rare earths, Britain remains dangerously exposed.”

It is the second time in a week that the government’s policy on China has been criticised by Byrne’s committee.

China has a stranglehold on the world’s supply of rare earths and other critical minerals, as well as their refined byproducts that are used in everything from military jets to car-locking systems and consumer products such as fridges and washing machines.

The committee heard that “the processing stage” was where the bottlenecks were, with China dominating the refining of seven categories of minerals, including refined lithium needed for electric vehicles and rare earths used in the fuselage and wings of military aircraft to help withstand temperature extremes.

MPs were told that demand for lithium alone would increase 45-fold between 2024 and 2030, leaving the UK in a high-risk dependency relationship with China.

The demand for rare earths needed for permanent magnets used in military jets and other applications would rise 16-fold in the same period as Britain was seeking to rebuild its military capabilities.

But with China capable of suddenly turning off rare earth supplies, as it did in 2025 , a dependency on Beijing was a strategic vulnerability for the UK economy and national security, the committee found.

Separate restrictions on legacy chips after a row over a Dutch intervention in the China-owned Nexperia left the European car industry “days away” from stoppages last October.

The EU, the US and other countries faced the same risk of supplies of rare earths being cut off by China, and the committee said the UK was not putting enough effort into finding alternative supplies.

Donald Trump secured a one-year reprieve on global export restrictions on rare earths from Xi Jinping in October last year. This was extended to January 2027 after the Chinese president’s recent visit to Washington.

However, the reprieve means the UK is at the mercy of US-China relations, the report suggests.

after newsletter promotion

The most “realistic” solution was for the UK to work closely with G7 partners, the rest of Europe and Indo-Pacific countries, to “aggregate demand” and bring in new suppliers.

The committee said its investigation was frustrated by lack of transparency by the government.

“Parliament has no visibility of the capabilities the government is seeking to protect, the vulnerabilities it has identified, or the projects it is backing to reduce risk,” it said.

The committee has drawn up a 10-point plan that includes: working to identify domestic mining; refining and recycling opportunities and their costs; a strategy to encourage business to reduce procurement from China; a plan to unlock investment; and assess planning and permitting processes that may prove a barrier to mining.

As it stood, the committee said it could not be confident the government could satisfy any of its 10 tests.

“The UK requires new institutional and financial muscle,” it concluded.

A government spokesperson denied it did not have a critical minerals strategy saying it was delivering £400m “to ramp up domestic production and recycling” and forge new international partnerships. “Our strategy also sets clear goals for 2035, including meeting 10% of demand through domestic production and 20% through recycling, with no more than 60% of any critical minerals coming from any single country,” they added.
